Our research uncovered significant, extensive cosmic-ray anisotropies at extremely high energies, exceeding 4 EeV, which weren't readily apparent in earlier findings. To achieve this discovery, we utilized detailed information about cosmic-ray orientations, collected from over 90% of the signal detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory's surface detectors, with a specific focus on areas around the celestial poles. By combining these data with two distinct perspectives, or "views," of the sky, we constructed a comprehensive picture of cosmic-ray flow patterns. We identified a predominant direction of enhanced cosmic-ray density, labeled the "footprint," at a latitude of negative 16 degrees, along with two distinct regions of decreased density: one at positive 26 degrees and another at negative 56 degrees, relative to the footprint. These regions, or "baskets," exhibit reduced cosmic-ray densities by 6.5% and 11.2% respectively, in comparison to the surrounding areas. The significance of these discoveries was confirmed through a comprehensive test, correcting for any potential biases. This research focuses on optimizing the data transfer rate in underwater fiber communications by utilizing a decision-feedback equalizer (DFE) technique. However, the performance of DFE is impaired due to the prevalence of burst errors caused by malfunctioning amplifier sections in the underwater transmission system. To enhance the effectiveness of DFE, we propose a new error-correction method called the partial burst-error transmission mitigation (PBETM) scheme. PBETM was successfully demonstrated in actual underwater fiber communications trials. Compared to standard DFE methods, PBETM showed significant rate-transmission rate improvements in both on-ground and underwater transmissions. Specifically, PBETM achieved a 50% greater data rate in underwater transmissions and a 25% greater data rate in on-ground transmissions, compared to the baseline DFE. These results indicate that the PBETM scheme can substantially enhance the transmission capacity of underwater fiber communications. Furthermore, we analyze various amplifier configurations to determine their impact on transmission performance. The findings can be applied to optimize the design of underwater fiber communications systems. The PBETM scheme is also compatible with other error-correcting techniques, such as forward error correction (FEC). Deep Learning-based models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) achieve high accuracy in time-series data analysis but can be vulnerable to over-parameterization. This research introduces a new trimming algorithm called 'Trimming In Time' (PIT) to reduce unnecessary parameters in TCNs by identifying and removing redundant network nodes. Compared to existing trimming methods, PIT maintains or even enhances performance while significantly decreasing the node count and subsequent computational costs. Our findings show that PIT effectively removes 5-20% of unnecessary parameters with only 0.5% probability of incorrect trimming, significantly outperforming alternative methods. To apply PIT to larger datasets, a new 'Early Trimming' algorithm is proposed, demonstrating its efficacy in reducing parameters by ~15% when data is abundant. Comprehensive experiments validate the efficacy of PIT in various real-world scenarios and network configurations. With the ability to minimize 1D TCN parameters by up to 30% without compromising accuracy, models like EfficientTCNs achieve a critical performance improvement of 4.3% in the Physionet-2017 dataset. This research provides a practical solution for trimming TCNs in real-world applications, making it suitable for use in emerging applications like medical diagnosis and cloud services. Count data often exhibit fluctuating patterns due to seasonal influences or sudden shifts, presenting a clear case for a dynamic model. Traditional methods for modeling count data usually rely on constant mean structures, which can fail to capture these changes. In contrast, the proposed dynamic Poisson autoregressive (DPAR) model of varying order adapts to changing patterns by continuously updating its lag structure, achieving a similar effect to the quasi-maximum likelihood estimation method used in Gaussian VAR models. A simulation investigation validates the suggested Estimating, Testing, and Iterative Refining (ETIAR) procedure, which facilitates parameter estimation and lag structure determination for the DPAR model. A real-world analysis of crime rates in Berlin, Germany, serves as a concrete application for the DPAR model, showcasing its capacity to model data with seasonal fluctuations and sharp transitions. A comparative analysis with alternative dynamic models, including the CAPAR and BAMAR models, is also presented, highlighting the DPAR model's effectiveness in modeling data with seasonal changes, sharp transitions, and excess variability. A R package named 'dparr' has been developed to execute the ESTIAR algorithm and the related lag structure refinement iterative procedure. Furthermore, a overview of the package's content and a detailed description of its functionality can be found in the user manual provided. A discussion on several research avenues related to the DPAR model has also been initiated in the paper's concluding section. A further development of the DPAR model is a Temporally-Varying Poisson Autoregressive (TV-PAR) model, which introduces a innovative iterative refinement step to the ESTIAR algorithm. This refinement step, based on a soft-thresholding technique, is designed to mitigate overdispersion by regulating the variance of the Poisson distribution. A simulation study validated the TV-PAR model's performance, and a real-world analysis of crime rates in Berlin, Germany, served as a concrete application for the model. A comparison with the DPAR model has also been conducted, and the results showed that the TV-PAR model is more efficient in estimating the parameters and the lag structure, but the DPAR model is more effective in modeling data with seasonal fluctuations and sharp transitions. Our proposed Neural Description Fields (NDFs) model creates a comprehensive 3D object representation by offering a probabilistic framework that generates various useful outputs, such as 2D sketches, 3D coordinates, and semantic labels, all tied to the object's physical properties and receive guidance from supervisory data with multiple attributes. This object representation is expressed as a probability distribution defined over the special Euclidean group (SE(3)), which encapsulates the object's positional and rotational aspects. To construct this representation, we develop a novel SE(3)-equivariant neural network that leverages graph neural networks and attention mechanisms to focus on critical object components and relationships. Training NDFs involves optimizing a primary task and several auxiliary objectives, utilizing both object description data and 3D-2D pair datasets, to create a robust and versatile object model. Our experiments validate NDFs' capacity for creating precise and generalizable 3D object models, surpassing traditional regression-based methods and demonstrating impressive performance in cross-view recognition and real-image projection tasks. Furthermore, NDFs' semantic-aware design enables seamless extension to category-level modeling via a simple yet effective approach. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/vita-256/neural-description-fields. This paper's distinctive features include numerous novel contributions: introducing SE(3)-equivariant 3D convolutional neural networks, integrating 3D-2D pair datasets into object description learning, a straightforward yet effective approach for extending NDFs to category-level modeling, and several novel experiments, including a real-world application in augmented reality. These innovations will also be explored in future research areas such as cross-domain generalization and the inclusion of physical simulations. This paper presents the results of a calorimeter redesign study for the SiD Detector, focusing on the forward section. In the original design, the forward section's liquid silicon sensors are arranged in a wedge-shaped layout with horizontal layers. However, this study proposes replacing the horizontal layers with layers oriented at 20 degrees to the forward direction. Additionally, the design's readout cells' sizes are being reduced from 1x1 cm^2 to 3x3 cm^2 to improve resolution. This redesigned forward section is expected to yield enhanced photon and electron energy recovery, along with increased hadron containment, without significant changes to the detector's overall size and weight. This redesign also offers potential benefits for upgrade paths, such as the addition of forward hadron rejection through plastic scintillator layers or the incorporation of timing information. Furthermore, the redesigned calorimeter's properties are compatible with the SiD Tracker's magnetic field, and the overall design is compatible with the SiD's central magnet. The proposed redesign holds promise for the SiD Detector, especially in its ability to provide precise energy and momentum measurements, which are crucial for the detector's sensitivity to dark matter and other rare processes. The Gigahertz-Optical Reference Frame Experiment (GORE) is a promising initiative to link optical and radio observations. GORE involves finding a radio curve that matches a moving optical pattern from a distance lens, created when a black hole warps space-time. Researchers have now published GORE findings based on 1.4 GHz data from the Very Large Array and 8200 lens candidates from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. From these, 14 events with distinct optical and radio signals have been used to determine a radio curve that a moving optical image must follow. By comparing this curve with others found through radio observations of radio lenses, researchers have identified a massive structure at approximately 1.5 billion light-years in length, but have not yet been able to determine its mass. This massive structure may be a cluster of colliding matter systems, and could also be a web-like feature associated with a large hole in the universe's matter distribution. Further study is needed to resolve uncertainties and improve the accuracy of mass measurements. Additionally, more sensitive radio observations of radio lenses discovered through GORE could provide valuable information about a related phenomenon, the absorption of radio signals by matter systems between Earth and a distant radio lens. This could offer new insights into the extension of a dark matter-dominated region in a universe region and the matter systems within it. Recently, deep learning techniques have been successful in determining a object's pose. However, calculating the full degree of freedom (DoF) pose relies heavily on correspondence information between 3D points on the object and 2D image coordinates, a task plagued by ambiguity and errors. Furthermore, traditional methods based on 3D clustering or segmentation struggle to account for pose changes. To address these challenges, this research proposes a novel deep learning framework, called DeepHMap++, which utilizes merged projection clustering and correspondence learning to determine a object's full DoF pose from monocular images. DeepHMap++ utilizes a multi-head correspondence network to establish accurate correspondences and a 3D clustering module that leverages image projections to refine the object's 3D clustering, thereby enabling robust pose estimation across various orientations, locations, and scales. Experimental results on multiple public benchmarks demonstrate DeepHMap++'s superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods. To overcome this constraint, we've developed an innovative technique that incorporates a highly efficient acoustic wave guiding substance, often used in sensing applications, to expand the detection area. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that TIRAL-based lenses can broaden the detection area by a minimum of 7 times with no adverse effects on spatial resolution. Furthermore, TIRAL-based lenses were successfully integrated into a PA breast imaging system, yielding accurate reconstructions of small objects and realistic breast phantoms. This breakthrough could potentially enable high-resolution PA imaging across larger areas of the breast. Additionally, we've investigated alternative acoustic lens substances with varying refractive indices and found that TIRAL's specific properties provide the ideal balance for optimal performance. While TIRAL's low losses make it suitable for repeated use at high intensities, further research is needed to fully assess its safety in photoacoustic imaging applications. Overall, this work provides a groundbreaking solution to expanding the detection area in photoacoustic imaging and may also be adapted for other imaging modalities. Furthermore, we've established that silicon oxide-based TIRAL can function effectively and efficiently within typical PA imaging parameter ranges. This includes refractive indices between 1.5 to 2.0, pulse durations from 10 seconds to 1 millisecond, and frequencies between 10 MHz to 50 MHz. Additionally, we've discovered that TIRAL's high surface energy and water droplet size of less than 100 nanometers contribute to its acoustic wave guiding capabilities. This has significant implications for the design of enhanced acoustic lens substances used in sensitive applications such as photoacoustic imaging. While silicon oxide-based TIRAL offers several advantages over other acoustic lens substances, further research is needed to fully assess its safety in photoacoustic imaging applications. approach that leverages a learning-based strategy in conjunction with raw
image processing principles. Our method is unique in that it utilizes two
complementary processes: a learning-based process that utilizes a collaborative
deblurring, demosaicing, and denoising model; and a non-deblurred image
transform that makes use of the characteristics of raw images. A transformation
block that converts raw images into deblurred, demosaiced, and denoised images is
then learned via a end-to-end approach. We assess the effectiveness of our raw
image processing approach that combines learning and traditional techniques,
noting that it outperforms existing learning-based and non-learning approaches. Our
method also yields competitive results on tasks that assume deblurred, demosaiced,
and denoised raw images, demonstrating robustness to misaligned deblurring,
demosaicing, and denoising. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach is
efficient and has a relatively low memory footprint. Our code is available at
https://github.com/ghm-2020/RAW. Our collaborative deblurring, demosaicing, and
denoising model consists of three components, each of which is a transformation
block that is learned via backpropagation with the aid of the algebraic
reconstruction technique (ART). Our demosaicing model makes use of the unique
pattern of raw images, leveraging the characteristics of raw images by treating
each raw image pixel as the sum of four neighboring pixels with the weights of
$\frac{1}{4}$. Our demosaicing model is a non-learning, four-layer transverse
filter that is analogous to the bicubic filter, with the exception of the last
layer, which is an identity filter, in contrast to the bicubic filter, which is

image formation model, which is a extension of the disordered slice image
deblurring model introduced in reference [32]. The difference between the two

single-sensor model, in contrast to the disordered slice image formation model,

Furthermore, we determine the modified form of the Laplace-Beltrami operator when the Minkowski metric is changed to an Einstein metric and establish the relationship with conformal metrics. Our findings also reveal how the revised formula facilitates the definition of a fundamental solution for the Laplace-Beltrami operator in transformed Minkowski spacetimes. Building on these results, we then generalize the concept of $R$-Minkowski spacetimes, defining a new class of spacetimes characterized by a linear transformation of the Minkowski metric in Euclidean space. Ultimately, we establish the connection between the revised formula and the concept of a fundamental solution in these generalized $R$-Minkowski spacetimes. Additionally, we explore how the policy of linear transformation being non-degenerate can be relaxed. Our findings are further verified by specific examples of $R$-Minkowski spacetimes, including examples of Einstein and conformally flat spacetimes. This study seeks to offer explanations and a predictive model for the seal performance of spheres moving through a fluid at moderate speeds. Unlike the well-understood regimes of high-speed flow, medium-speed flow patterns are complicated and involve both laminar and turbulent aspects. In this study, we propose a theoretical model that combines elements of both fluid dynamics phenomena to explain the behavior of spheres moving through a fluid at medium speeds. Additionally, we provide supporting evidence from both previous research and new experimental data. Our research suggests that the seal performance of spheres moving through a fluid at medium speeds can be described by a dimensionless number known as the Reynolds number, and that a predictive model for this performance relies on the critical surface tension barrier model, but with modifications to account for the impact of fluid friction. Furthermore, we propose a new methodology for determining the contact angle of spheres, and demonstrate to what extent the proposed model can be an alternative to existing methods for calculating the seal performance of spheres moving through a fluid. This research is relevant to a wide range of applications involving spheres moving through a fluid, and the models and methods presented could be adapted for use with other geometric shapes that form a seal with a fluid. Additionally, the proposed model for the seal performance of spheres could be a starting point for the development of more complex models, such as those that account for multiple spheres moving through a fluid at different speeds. This study confirms the significance of fluid friction in determining the seal performance of spheres moving through a fluid, and highlights the need for further research into the behavior of spheres moving through a fluid at medium speeds, particularly with regards to flow patterns and the critical surface tension barrier model. Lastly, we outline potential areas for further research into this topic. This study is an extension of previous research presented at the 2019 STLE Annual Meeting in Detroit, Michigan, USA. As AI models grow in size and complexity, inference scheduling becomes a performance-critical component, largely unaffected by hardware advancements. Current research focuses on integrating multiple accelerators into a single system to improve overall throughput, but fails to address a significant constraint: many hardware components, such as FPGAs and ASICs, have limited physical isolation, forcing co-located applications to share resources. This research introduces a novel formulation that minimizes confidence in meeting deadline requirements for tasks that can be executed on hardware components with physical isolation, such as FPGA boards, and combines this with an iterative algorithm and limited hardware expertise. Evaluations using real hardware and applications demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing methods and surpasses theoretical optimal solutions. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. While significant progress has been made in recent years, especially with the application of deep learning, NER remains challenging, primarily due to the complexities of language and the inherent difficulties inherent to all natural languages. NER is generally treated as a classification problem, where each token is classified as an independent entity. However, this approach overlooks the inherent relationships and structures within languages and the hierarchical nature of entities. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel nested NER model that analyzes language as a holistic structure, with which we participated in the BERT NER Challenge at the 12th CIPR Conference and achieved the best results overall. Furthermore, our model's performance was consistently superior to existing approaches, demonstrating the efficacy of modeling language as a holistic structure. Additionally, our work provides a theoretical foundation for the development of more sophisticated neural pipeline NLP systems. We employ tropical geometry to count the number of bitangents to a surface quartic, demonstrating that this count is rational in the coefficients of the quartic. Furthermore, we utilize $\mathbb{A}^1$-motivic techniques to determine the formula for the number of bitangents, previously established by Prasad, in a more general context. Building upon our findings, we calculate the number of real bitangents for a surface quartic, extending the results from our earlier research. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the virtual and actual numbers of bitangents, revealing that the ratio of these numbers can be expressed as a sum of roots of polynomials related to the Coxeter numbers of the Weyl group of type $E_8$. This statistical analysis of the number of bitangents to a surface quartic provides new insights, extending our earlier work with Charles Favreau and Matthew Kilgore.

While numerous online platforms offer support for multiple languages, they often restrict expressions like code-mixing, considering them "abuse". This paper encourages developers to acknowledge code-mixing as a normal feature of multilingual communication, offering suggestions on how NLP systems can better understand and respond effectively to such language. We also highlight potential applications and provide a starting point for further research in this area. The spread of misinformation across the United States has been scrutinized in previous research, yet a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon is still lacking. This study aims to illuminate the dissemination of misinformation in the country by applying network analysis to Reddit user interactions. Our results indicate that a diverse range of topics spreads misinformation across diverse geographic areas, whereas certain arrangements of population centers are more effective at disseminating false information related to news and entertaining content. Conversely, user engagement on Reddit is less efficient at disseminating misinformation compared to other topics, and this variation is particularly noticeable in urban areas - where user curiosity is not enough to override the fact-checking tendencies of Redditors. Our research also reveals that users in different geographic regions tend to share false information with those in nearby areas, but this pattern is less pronounced in urban settings. Lastly, we discover that reducing the emphasis on user community and the robustness of online networks may lead to the unwinding of geographic arrangements' impact on the dissemination of misinformation. Our study's insights have valuable implications for the design of information systems and strategies to contain the spread of false information in online communities. Teaching robots via demonstration and feedback is a crucial skill for human instructors, however, the process is often inefficient due to significant knowledge gaps between what the instructor intends to convey and what the robot actually learns. The underlying issue lies in the fact that instructors typically convey their intent through unspecific and indirect language, unrelated to the robot's programming. To bridge this gap, our study focuses on the audio components of human instructions as providing critical, albeit implicit, information to the instructor about the task at hand. We analyzed video recordings of humans instructing and operating various robotic arms via demonstration and language, discovering that human speech reflects the spatial and temporal structures of the task natively. We developed a novel, task-agnostic framework that learns to recognize the underlying patterns in human language and use them as cues to predict the robot's performance. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to data from three diverse task sets. The findings of this research have significant implications for enhancing the efficacy of human instructions to robots, potentially creating self-guided learning pathways and optimizing instructional audio recorded from humans. We are currently exploring methods to integrate this research with structural analysis of human language and visual components of the instruction videos. These extensions are expected to further improve the ability of our model to predict the robot's performance and facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of human instruction patterns. We are open to collaborating with researchers in the machine learning and human-robot interaction communities to accelerate progress in this area. We have already released our model and data sets, which can be accessed at https://github.com/PRMLab/AudioCodebook. We anticipate that future research in this area will contribute to creating more versatile and adaptive human-robot collaboration systems. The foundation theorem in the theory of the Coxeter groups is a significant and widely utilized result that provides a significant insight into the structure of the group. It has numerous applications in the field of combinatorial theory, geometry, and algebra. However, its proof relies heavily on the characteristics of the finite Coxeter groups, specifically their reflection representation, which is an irreducible permutation matrix. This essential property is lacking in the infinite hyperbolic Coxeter groups, as their reflection representation can be a reducible matrix. As a result, many previously established foundation-related results are no longer applicable in this setting. This paper addresses this gap by providing a more general foundation theorem that the Coxeter groups form a universal system of generators, and it proves additional properties related to foundation, including a chordless triangle condition and a 3-distance condition. This general foundation theorem can be applied to a broad category of Coxeter groups, which includes the finite Coxeter groups, the classical Weyl groups, the affine Weyl groups, the extended affine Weyl groups, the Tits buildings of type A_D,D, as well as the Coxeter groups associated with a tree. This paper also introduces the concept of a "good" Coxeter matrix, which can be used to describe the graph of a Coxeter system. It then utilizes this concept to prove yet another more general foundation theorem. Furthermore, this paper explores both necessary and sufficient conditions for a graph to satisfy the 3-distance condition, as well as the condition of having no "bad" minors. Living kidney donors undergo rigorous medical evaluation to ensure the safety of both the donor and the recipient. Once a compatible match is found, the focus shifts to other factors such as kidney quality, waiting time, and the social connection between the donor and recipient. This study aims to investigate the ideal acceptance of kidneys that wouldn't normally work, with the goal of increasing the pool of available kidneys and potentially reduce waiting times for transplant patients. Using a simulation model, we analyzed the ideal acceptance of kidneys from incompatible living donors and deceased donors, and found that accepting kidneys from incompatible living donors with a higher EMD (estimated mismatch degree) results in increased waiting times and reduced transplant success rates. Therefore, the ideal acceptance of kidneys from incompatible living donors would be zero. This policy could also increase the pool of available kidneys from incompatible living donors, although the benefit is more significant for deceased donors. It's worth noting that this policy may disadvantage African American and Hispanic transplant patients, as they have a harder time finding compatible living donors. To address this issue, a more complex solution, such as kidney quality assessment, may be necessary. Using data from the United Network for Organ Transplantation (UNOS), we analyzed factors that increase the likelihood of a kidney match from an incompatible living donor, and found that a higher donor-rated quality, better post-donation health, and a stronger social connection between the donor and recipient can all raise the chances of accepting the kidney. We also found that the willingness to accept kidneys from incompatible living donors varies by transplant center, with some centers being more open to such offers. Finally, we propose a new classification system for evaluating the quality of kidneys from incompatible living donors, and suggest conducting a randomized controlled trial to test the ideal acceptance policy. If successful, this policy could increase the availability of kidneys for transplant patients in need. This study provides valuable insights for transplant centers, living donor chains, and kidney exchange networks, as well as UNOS and the medical community at large. This model encompasses a wide range of alternative gravity theories, including $f(R)$ theories, TeVeS, and $\Lambda$CDM, among others. By transforming the gravitational potential into a conformally equivalent form, we are able to simulate n-body systems without solving the Einstein field equations, thus allowing for the simulation of complex systems with just a few galaxy pairwise properties. We then utilize these artificial datasets in n-body simulations to investigate the effects of alternative gravity on galaxy clustering, including the distribution of galaxy pairwise odds and the anisotropy of galaxy clustering. Our results show that in order to replicate the characteristics of real galaxy distributions, any alternative gravity theory must closely resemble $\Lambda$CDM at the highly nonlinear scales of galaxy interactions. Furthermore, we discover that the Conformal Linking Model is capable of distinguishing between different alternative gravity theories based on their effects on galaxy clustering. Hill, where an attempt was made to consistently integrate general covariance and the Standard Model of particle physics. Our study on the Conformal Linking Model facilitates a more in-depth analysis of galaxy clustering under modified gravity, acknowledging any potential biases in our findings, given that the Model's behavior within galaxy clusters may be influenced by the Model's own cluster-specific parameters, derived from its global properties. Furthermore, we explore the impact of different detection settings on cluster identification and observe the detector's ability to adapt to changing cluster dynamics. Our detection method proves particularly useful for clustering regions that exhibit inter-neuron connectivity different from the rest of the network. We examine the aggregation of particles in a two-dimensional lattice fluid with varied connectivity patterns, including a fully connected grid and several less connected lattices. Unlike typical models that feature extensive bonding between nearby particles, our model sees particles connect to a much smaller number of nearest neighbors, forming isolated triads instead of stable pairs. This distinction causes pairs to dissociate into separate monomers at higher temperatures, a contrast to typical two-state binding curves. Conversely, in optimal conditions, a given species can multiply into clusters of any size due to the extensive connectivity of triads, producing exponential cluster distributions. This property enables the derivation of a cluster size exponent of 1.25 for our model, averaging 1.26 when calculating the exponent for different lattices. A proposed Hamiltonian for our model successfully reproduces the observed triad and monomer behavior and provides a way to alter the model's connectivity. Changing the Hamitonian's parameters can yield clusters of a specific size in a process we term 'cluster engineering'. Finally, we explore the potential for our model to represent the behavior of catalytically active molecules that can form bonds with multiple atoms. This interpretation is supported by our findings that in some situations, a given species can dominate the composition of clusters of a specific size, even when starting from a random distribution. This phenomenon raises the possibility that the model could be used to design catalysts by clustering them in desired arrangements. A larger scope for our model's triad-based connectivity may also provide a solution to the issue of unsolved clusters observed in some of our experiments, where certain sizes failed to converge despite extensive computation. The unexplored area of ultra-high energy physics involves photons with energies above $10^{17}$ eV. Since the solar magnetic field significantly affects directional photons in this energy range, we developed a system to simulate their creation and propagation. We present a formula for calculating the interaction rate of these high-energy photons with solar magnetic field fluctuations, and demonstrate our method with computer simulations, also offering a simplified approximation for practical use. We anticipate that future experiments involving ultra-high energy photon detection will be sensitive to this process, and potentially reveal information about primordial cosmic rays. We also propose an experiment consisting of a next-generation, multi-component, quasi-isotropic array of optical detectors that could significantly improve our understanding of these high-energy photons. We estimate the detectable flux of such photons to be in the order of $10^{6}$ photons per day, and predict that even a modest improvement in sensitivity could lead to a major breakthrough in this field. We conclude that while our method can already provide useful insights, further development is necessary to fully optimize its performance. We discuss this optimization, along with other aspects of our method, and also address some open questions and potential areas for further research. We also outline the technical specifications for an experimental setup that could significantly benefit from a more sophisticated method. We conclude that even though our method can already provide some useful information, further development is necessary to fully optimize its performance, and that in the meantime, considering a more sophisticated method for the experimental setup that we propose could be very beneficial. We hope that this proposal could also serve as an example of an interesting research topic for young physicists. To raise awareness about the importance of open access to genomics data, the third annual Genome Stanford Meeting was organized as a webinar due to COVID-19 restrictions. This meeting brought together experts from top Asian universities to collaborate and share knowledge. In the context of this webinar, our team participated in a series of challenges designed to combine genomic information with genome-wide association studies to predict certain traits. These predictions involved rich data formats such as expression and methylation profiles, as well as case-control GWAS datasets for 18 different characteristics. To tackle this task, we employed an ensemble of feature selection and machine learning algorithms to identify potential regulatory mechanisms underlying the traits in question. Our solutions not only outperformed the existing state-of-the-art models but also also provided valuable insights into potential targets and pathways associated with each characteristic, as evident from the enriched gene sets obtained from the challenge results. Furthermore, our predictions for the traits "body mass index" and "type 2 diabetes" revealed novel potential associations with certain tissues and life stages, as reflected in the challenge's secondary questions. In the case of "bmi", our model indicated that fat tissue plays a crucial role, while for "type 2 diabetes", our results suggested that predicting the condition in adipose tissue is more challenging than in the liver. Additionally, our team observed that for at least three of the traits - "bladder cancer", "colorectal cancer", and "type 2 diabetes" - existing genome-wide association studies lacked a comprehensive understanding of the underlying genetics. can complicate the task of developing automated language systems. To date, NLP
models have been primarily fine-tuned on corpora with uniform linguistic
characteristics, which may not adequately prepare them for navigating the
semantic diversity inherent in human discourse. To address this challenge, we
introduce the Discourse NLI Task, which involves presenting NLI systems with a
single sentence hypothesis and two diverse supporting sentences from a range
of contexts, including but not limited to, argumentative, conversational, and
scientific texts. By incorporating a range of supporting sentences with
differing semantic features, this task aims to evaluate NLI systems' ability to
navigate the semantic diversity inherent in human discourse. Our research spans
three aspects: first, we assess the discourse norms underlying each context;
second, we examine the semantic profiles of each context; third, we introduce a
new context-aware framework for the NLI task and showcase its superiority over
existing models. Ultimately, our Discourse NLI Data aims to contribute a new
corpus to the NLI domain, which can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the
robustness and generalizability of NLI systems in the face of semantic variety
and diversity. This corpus comprises 393K instances, including 144K discourse
triads labeled for semantic similarity or contrast, in addition to 249K sentence
hypothesis-discourse triads. We also introduce Discodif, a context-aware
unified model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on our Discourse NLI
Data, surpassing conventional models like BERT and RoBERTa. Notably, our research
reveals that while BERT and RoBERTa exhibit context-specific knowledge, they
still struggle with generalization, which is not a concern for Discodif. We
believe that successful NLI systems in the future will need to be capable of
handling the semantic diversity inherent in human discourse, as evidenced by our
results. Our research and data are open-source and available at https://github.com/Asr-2021/semantic variety in discourse. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI applications, especially those involving image recognition tasks. However, most conventional techniques often rely on well-labeled training datasets, which is not always the case in practice. In situations where new classes continually emerge and existing ones disappear, the task becomes one of incremental learning (IL). A subcategory of IL is the class-incremental learning (CIL) task, in which the model must adapt to new classes while forgetting existing ones. A notable constraint of CIL is the presence of unlabeled data from previous classes. A more complex and less-studied aspect of CIL is the problem of dealing with imbalanced data. In the case of CIL, the issue of data imbalance arises when there is a significant discrepancy in the number of training examples between old and new classes. If left unaddressed, this phenomenon can result in the model exhibiting a bias towards the new classes and, as a consequence, failing to recognize existing ones. Various techniques aim to rectify this shortcoming; nonetheless, a comprehensive evaluation of these methods in the context of deep neural network-based CIL has yet to be conducted. This research conducts an in-depth assessment of seven different regularization techniques that can mitigate the data imbalance issue in deep neural network-based CIL. The evaluation was conducted using a subset of the CORe50 benchmark dataset and comprised 2000 training examples from 20 progressively revealed classes, with each class defined by 100 samples from 10 different views. The study found that three techniques--online hard positive mining (OHNM), focusing on easy examples (EE) and re-sampling (RS) - consistently outperformed the baseline approach. Moreover, our analysis uncovered the inherent link between these methods and energy-based models, suggesting that OHNM and EE can be viewed as variants of contrastive learning. In the near future, there will be a high demand for robotic assistants to care for elderly and disabled individuals in their homes. These robots will likely require the ability to efficiently move around on two feet, navigating various environments. Our investigation compared the effectiveness of three different approaches to propulsion-assisted bipedal movement, which involve the use of flat and tapered feet in relation to the direction of travel. We particularly examined how each method handles unexpected obstacles and slippery floors. Our findings indicate that the strategy using a tapered foot in the direction of travel yields the greatest benefits in terms of energy conservation and resistance to twisting, however it proves less capable of recovering from slipouts. On the other hand, the method with a flat foot in the direction of travel demonstrates superior performance in recovering from slipouts but fails to recover from twisting and proves less energetically efficient. Lastly, the strategy with a flat foot against the direction of travel exhibits the worst results in regards to energy conservation and resistance to twisting but exhibits intermediate capabilities in recovering from slipouts and twisting. Ultimately, the approach with a tapered foot in the direction of travel appears to be the most suitable for propulsion-assisted bipedal movement. Recent studies have shown that in data centers, the latency of CPU instructions does not solely determine application performance, but rather it is often dominated by memory and storage access. As a result, in-order execution of CPU instructions may be optimized without compromising program behavior. We present a new technique called HyperDegrade, which involves dividing a high-speed CPU bus into multiple lower-speed buses to reduce memory and storage access latency. By utilizing multiple instruction streams, HyperDegrade can still provide elevated single-thread performance. Our research involves designing and simulating three different HyperDegrade variants, but a detailed explanation of these designs is not provided here. Simulations indicate that HyperDegrade can reduce energy consumption by a factor of 5 to 10 while maintaining performance comparable to in-order out-of-order CPUs, which serve as the baseline system. Furthermore, HyperDegrade can also provide a significant increase in energy-efficiency improvement over time, especially in large data centers. As a result, HyperDegrade may provide a viable solution for enhancing the energy-efficiency of future high-speed CPUs. However, this potential benefit also creates a significant challenge: developing a comprehensive understanding of global IR behavior in quantities derived from amplitude-driven resummation. Additionally, we explore the connection between globally IR-safe structures and soft-collinear effective theory and discuss potential extensions to the theory's scope. Unlike more common conditions like dilated cardiomyopathy, where extensive training datasets are available, our experimentation involves training and testing models on relatively small datasets of $256\times256$ pixel images obtained from cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Power spectrum analysis is a widely used data reduction technique in various studies, often employed to extract information by evaluating the intensity of periodic signals at different frequencies. However, many natural processes exhibit combined periodic signals resulting from the interaction of two underlying cycles, as seen in the 43.41 Hz frequency found in the EEG of a person's ears in response to a sound, which is linked to the half-wave of the 86.82 Hz frequency generated by the two ears responding to distinct sound frequencies. Nevertheless, research indicates that this frequency is higher, likely 103 Hz, 11 times 9.3 Hz, a frequency associated with the respiratory rate. Unfortunately, conventional power spectrum analysis around a single central frequency suffers from sidelobe contamination, as seen in the case of 103 Hz, where the detected power originates from 9.3 Hz rather than 11 times 9.3. To address this issue, we propose a method that evaluates power ratios at multiple reference frequencies within a wider frequency range, reducing sidelobe contamination and enhancing the detection of weak signals. This approach is applied to an empirical dataset obtained from a person's EEG during auditory visual stimulation, resulting in the identification of distinct power ratio frequencies with enhanced sensitivity and specificity. Notably, our research demonstrates that power ratio analysis is more effective than traditional power spectrum analysis in one dimension. We anticipate that this novel approach will be valuable in the analysis of complex datasets from studies involving multiple sensory modalities. As such, we have created an R package named 'bimod' to execute power ratio analysis in one and two dimensions. The 'bimod' package is designed to execute a wide range of power ratio frequencies and ratios, including spectral edge frequency, as well as low-frequency power ratio and high-frequency power ratio. We believe that our proposed framework will be beneficial in the analysis of complex datasets from multichannel recordings. We have integrated the 'ggfortify' package's 'ggfortis()' function, allowing for the creation of interactive 3D plots generated by the 'plotly' package. However, $n$-gram models possess intuitive parameters that provide insight into language structure and have applications in spoken language understanding, such as topic identification and paraphrase detection. While neural language models can be trained with task-specific models, their intermediate representations remain understudied. Our research reversely approaches this issue by training a task-specific model with $n$-gram-based neural networks and examining the learned representations. The results show that the intermediate representations of $n$-gram-based neural networks are more accurate than those of full neural language models, while providing similar or better performance in downstream tasks including spoken language understanding, topic identification, and paraphrase detection. Furthermore, we propose a residual learning framework that combines the strengths of both $n$-gram models and neural language models. The findings indicate that the parameterized intermediate representations of neural language models are not a universal improvement over $n$-gram models, as they are highly dependent on the specific task and dataset used. A common approach to this problem involves training neural networks to identify face features, but many existing methods train on heavily preprocessed training data, which doesn't account for real-world applications. Additionally, most existing networks are treated as separate components for alignment and reconstruction, rather than end-to-end systems, which can lead to information loss and difficult optimization. In the context of linear models and time series data, due to the presence of strong dependencies, the usual asymptotic behavior may break down, leading to an atypical situation where the population risk minimizer is not unique. This issue becomes particularly challenging in an over-parameterized setting, characterized by an excess number of features relative to the number of observations. In such cases, traditional consistency results may not apply, and the usual asymptotic theory may be compromised. This paper seeks to fill this gap by investigating the properties of an estimator formed by the optimization of a linear model when the data follows an autoregressive process, specifically focusing on the situation where the optimal risk minimizer is not distinct. The primary goal of this research is to establish an explicit condition on the matrix of regression coefficients that ensures the estimated coefficients converge to a unique, albeit irregular, minimizer of the population risk function. The condition is shown to be a necessary and sufficient requirement for the proposed estimator to converge to a non-irregular minimizer. The results are then extended to other time series models, such as ARCH and GARCH models, by utilizing a new approach that facilitates the application of a block circulant matrix property. The findings are also applicable to a wide range of over-determined linear models, including sparse regression and low-rank matrix completion, by leveraging the principles of convex optimization and regularized estimation. The established condition provides valuable insights into the optimal choice of regularization parameters, which can be made more flexible in accordance with the strength of dependencies in the data. The results are then validated through numerical examples, which demonstrate the advantages of the proposed estimator compared to existing methods, such as the least squares estimator in the presence of heteroscedastic errors and the LASSO estimator in sparse regression. A significant issue in optimizing Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) arises due to their inherent Hamiltonian dynamics, which can lead to convergent difficulties, especially when these networks are employed as optimal control policies. This problem is extensively explored and a theoretical framework is established to identify the conditions under which HNNs gradients can be acquired, thus enabling optimization using gradient-based methods. Our framework, in addition to providing a design guideline for HNNs, also reveals the circumstances in which obtaining HNNs gradients is impossible. To address the challenge of non-convergence in HNNs training, we propose a novel Hamiltonian Backpropagation (HBP) algorithm, which acquires HNNs gradients via a surrogate Hamiltonian dynamics while avoiding the computation of the Hessian matrix. The HBP algorithm is a more versatile solution that enables the optimization of HNNs without relying on the explicit specification of the Hamiltonian objective function. The HBP algorithm is a highly adaptable solution that enables the optimization of HNNs without relying on the explicit specification of the Hamiltonian objective function. Through comprehensive experiments and evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets, the performance of the HBP algorithm is compared with the standard bi-directional optimization method, resulting in consistent improvements achieved through the HBP algorithm. This innovation enables the identification of two distinct families of chains in $T^2 \times I$, which we call the "torus links" and "twisted torus links", whose quantum approximations converge at a rate specified by the volume hypothesis. This new invariant also detects and distinguishes between twisted torus links of various colors, a capability that conventional quantum invariants lack. This task, called melody captioning, demands a deep understanding of both music composition and language generation. Our study takes a novel approach by asking multiple groups of subjects to describe melodies, using both spoken and written responses. These descriptions are then used to train both a baseline neural network and a more advanced model tailored to the task's unique characteristics. When evaluated against these models and existing knowledge about the melodies, a more sophisticated neural network consistently produces more accurate results. Temporal activity detection in videos is identified as the creation of temporal boundaries to mark the start and end of ongoing activities. This study uncovers the common misconception in current approaches that videos naturally contain clearly defined activity periods and instead proves the opposite with a data-driven strategy. A novel framework called DCAN is introduced, relying on dual context consolidation to address this issue. This framework is unique in its ability to collect relevant timing information from positively and negatively labeled context contexts to accurately define activity duration. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through various context-aware design options and subsequent implementation in a learning-based strategy called Dual Context Consolidation Network (DCAN). Experimental results show that DCAN surpasses current state-of-the-art models in terms of precision and recall while also offering complementary insights through context analysis. Moreover, an open-source code for the proposed DCAN framework is made available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN. The framework's code is built using PyTorch and easily integratable into existing activity detection frameworks. Furthermore, an online benchmark called ActivityDuration has been established at https://activityduration.org/ to evaluate the performance of DCAN and other participating methods. This benchmark includes detailed codes for context consolidation and learning strategies based on dual context information. The establishment of this benchmark aims to elevate the understanding of activity duration from mere boundary prediction towards the more complex analysis of temporal patterns. This is the first study to define activity duration in videos through the context of activities, introduce the Dual Context Consolidation framework, and establish the ActivityDuration benchmark to advance research in this area. The expertise of renowned experts in the field has been sought, leading to several valuable feedback sessions and subsequent revisions to the submitted work. The novel framework of Dual Context Consolidation offers numerous potential applications, including the creation of engaging sports highlights by identifying the most thrilling moments, the development of tourism videos highlighting the temporal beauty of natural scenes, and the production of emotional music videos by detecting sad or happy periods. This study also explores the establishment of a new line of research called 'temporally-rich activity analysis' that goes beyond basic boundary prediction and instead focuses on analyzing the complex temporal dynamics within activities. The DCAN framework's versatility allows it to be adapted for use in various datasets, such as sports, facial expression recognition, and medical diagnosis from video recordings. A thorough examination of JET experiments and associated computational models has been carried out to gain a deeper understanding of these enigmatic events. It has been discovered that PTMs often develop from mode pairs linked to ERM and MHD interactions and characterized by close magnetic fieldline tracking. A study investigates the information filtering capabilities of Google's Web search, focusing on its impact on discovering new information. A critical aspect examined is the phenomenon of "hidden" or "occluded" information, which refers to pertinent data that cannot be found due to their inability to attract attention beyond a certain threshold. To evaluate this, a protocol was established where participant collectors search for information to reach a predetermined score, simulating the discovery of new information. The results show that a significant amount of hidden information exists, which grows as the threshold for attention decreases. Furthermore, the data indicates that Google's filtering reduces discovery efficiency by up to 73%, and the impact varies depending on topics. Interestingly, the information hidden the furthest from the top-ranking documents accounts for a minor 11% of all discoverable information. To validate these findings, the study was replicated with different participants and parameters, and the results showed consistent evidence of extensive information filtering, including the phenomenon of hidden information. The study's implications suggest that Google's filtering may undermine its effectiveness in discovering new information, particularly in academic settings where the goal is to find the most up-to-date information. The data also raise concerns about the reliability of Google's ability to prioritize essential information, and the study concludes by highlighting the need for further research into the information filtering capabilities of Google's Web search. This research paper proposes a novel approach to creating secure and robust controllers for complex nonlinear control systems. We introduce a new controller design framework based on Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) that can incorporate various input limitations found in real-world systems. Our key innovation includes two main contributions: first, we expand the applicability of CBFs to address a broader security concern, namely reaching a specific control barrier; second, we integrate multiple types of input restrictions, including their combinations, to create an 'composite' restriction that can be analyzed through a new'reaching intensity' function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through the design of an secure controller for a nonlinear helicopter aircraft system. Notably, this helicopter model exhibits an underactuated and non-minimum phase behavior, characteristic often found in robotic systems. Through simulation, we validate the performance of the controller in achieving setpoint targeting while ensuring the system reaches a specified control barrier and adheres to multiple types of input restrictions. Additionally, we explore the impact of various parameters, including the strength of the CBF and the severity of input restrictions, on the resulting secure controller. Overall, our research provides a foundation for creating safe and resilient controllers in complex high-dimensional systems. Finally, we conclude by highlighting potential future applications and challenges related to input constrained CBFs. This research was previously published in a conference proceedings paper presented at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC). Additionally, an extended version of this work can be found as an article in the IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control.

We introduce a novel mathematical framework, centered on graph-based representations, to analyze the underlying structure of condensed systems at equilibrium. Our approach is adaptable to multiple physical contexts and is particularly well-suited for investigating the microscopic aspects of phase transitions. Within this framework, we examine the relationship between graph-based structures, known as fabric spaces, and the varying configurations of interacting particles that give rise to these structures. Our key finding is that the microscopically-defined fabric spaces are homeomorphic to the space of pairwise interaction distances between particles, a relationship that is fundamentally rooted in the local, finite-range nature of particle interactions. As a consequence, we demonstrate that the graph-based structures underlying diverging families of Ginzburg-Landau theories share a common, universal feature: they are all characterized by an infinite number of degree-three vertices in their underlying graphs. Finally, we apply our framework to study the universality of physical processes in the vicinity of critical points and across critical interfaces. Our results are validated through numerical simulations and theoretical calculations for two different physical contexts. Additionally, we offer an intuitive explanation for the behavior of correlation lengths in condensed systems, and our framework also enables the analytical solution of some renormalization group equations. Our approach provides a new perspective on the physics of the renormalization group and the underlying structures giving rise to the behaviors observed in phase transitions. Our research is a result of the collaboration between physicists and mathematicians at the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Sciences during the "Physics and Mathematics in China" conference. Our work has since inspired a collaborative research project between Chinese institutions, led by Dr. Wei Chen, Dr. Jian Zhang, and Dr. Sheng-Jiang Chang. Our research has resulted in the publication of the paper "From fabric spaces to diverging triangulations" in the journal Science China Physics & Mathematics, as well as the posting of the paper on the arXiv preprint server. Our research has also been presented at the "Recent Developments in Statistical Mechanics" conference, and the "Recent Advances in Condensed Matter Physics" conference. Graph neural network sparsification has emerged as a highly effective technique to achieve both model compression and interpretation by limiting model parameters and eliminating unnecessary edges, respectively. While various sparsification methods are available, most are based on unsupervised pruning rules that may not guarantee optimal performance. In contrast, learning-based sparsification methods optimize model parameters and edges simultaneously, but are computationally expensive and challenging to optimize due to the non-convexity of graph neural networks. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel learned sparsification framework that combines the benefits of optimization-based and reduction-based sparsification methods. By applying this framework to various GNN tasks, we demonstrate its ability to create highly interpretable and efficient models that outperform existing state-of-the-art GNNs. Notably, our method achieves comparable performance to model-agnostic neural sparsification methods while providing substantial improvements in edge reduction. Moreover, the compact models produced by our method exhibit superior performance on various datasets, including the WebKB and PubMed datasets, particularly in the tasks of graph classification and multi-label classification. Overall, our learned sparsification framework offers a more efficient and effective approach to creating understandable and efficient GNNs. We have also introduced an open-source Python framework called GraphPrune, which provides an easy-to-use interface for and easy integration with popular GNN PyTorch modules. This framework includes our proposed learned sparsification framework, as well as various model compression and interpretation techniques. By utilizing a unified module structure and token-based argument passing, GraphPrune enables seamless incorporation of sparsification techniques into GNN training loops. This not only facilitates the exploration of various learned sparsification methods, but also enables the extension of the framework to address which model parameters to retain, a question that GraphPrune addresses under the umbrella of a novel technique called parameter sparsification. By incorporating both edge and parameter sparsification capabilities, GraphPrune provides a comprehensive solution for creating compact, interpretable, and efficient GNN models. However, in this paper we demonstrate that there exists a class of vectors for which the error margin decreases to $O(\sqrt{k \log N})$ when $N$ and $k$ are sufficiently large, and also outline an extension to the problem of finding the top $k$ elements in a matrix $A$ by recovering the top $k$ columns of $A$ which can be achieved with an increased sketch size of $k^2$. Moreover, this result applies to the popular Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma. Furthermore, a new technique called the'relaxation trick' is introduced which facilitates the development of more efficient algorithms that can tolerate a wider class of adaptive inputs with minimal additional overhead. As a result, a new algorithm is presented which can accurately recover the top $k$ elements of a $N$-dimensional vector in time $O(N \log N)$ when $N$ is much larger than $k$, and also an improved algorithm for solving the $L_1$ regularization problem which runs in time $O(N^2 \log N)$ for $N^2$ inputs. The techniques and the'relaxation trick' also lead to the development of a new algorithm called the 'two-sketch algorithm' which can solve the $L_1$ regularization problem with an information complexity of $O(k^2)$ for $N^2$ inputs by utilizing only $2k^2$ sketches size of $O(k \log N)$ each. A heat current applied to a type-II superconductor within its critical temperature range causes a shift in the distribution of vortices, generating an electric current that varies over time and space. This phenomenon is most pronounced when a Nernst response is induced by applying a weak electric field along the type-II superconductor's edges, resulting in a transverse Nernst effect that surpasses the ordinary transverse effect observed in the absence of vortices. Our research indicates that a strong, applied heat current can result in a persistent electric field within the superconductor's core, potentially leading to the expansion of the vortex core and a return current that opposes the applied heat current. This persistence of electric field may be described by a simplified model that involves a resistance born from the vortex core itself. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the vortex core's resistance can be measured using a variety of methods, including transverse transport and the tunneling splitting of the vortex core's spin state. A particularly useful method involves the measurement of transverse transport entropy, which provides insight into the vortex core's resistance and the temperature at which the resistance is minimized, as well as the temperature at which the superconductor's critical current is reached. Additionally, the relationship between the superconductor's thickness and the measurement of transverse transport entropy has been explored, revealing that the temperature at which the minimum resistance is reached increases in proportion to the superconductor's thickness. Lastly, the application of a strong electric field to the superconductor is shown to result in a widening of the vortex core's diameter and a shift in the location of the minimum resistance within the vortex core itself. This phenomenon is explained in the context of the superconductor's quasi-two-dimensional nature and the need for a more comprehensive theoretical model that takes this dimensionality into account. This model should also be applicable to other quasi-two-dimensional, type-II superconductors, including those with structural defects and applied pressures, as well as superconductors transitioning from a finite to an infinite magnetic field. To study this phenomenon, we constructed a chamber filled with sand and a layer of fluid, then used a cylindrical solid to compress its surface and observe the behavior of the granular layer as it's forced into a sinusoidal pattern. By comparing and contrasting these two situations, we demonstrated that drag asymmetry, an irregularity in the flow pattern, occurs in both scenarios and is significantly more pronounced when the cylinder is partially submerged. Additionally, we found that the critical Reynolds number, which indicates the onset of drag asymmetry, is lower when the cylinder is partially submerged and is affected by the fluid's viscosity in an unexpected manner. Lastly, we proposed a method to calculate the drag asymmetry in this context and validated our approach with available data. This research provides insight into the complex interplay of forces at play and may have implications for the study of flow patterns in other scenarios. When working with experimental data from random processes, reducing noise is often essential for drawing conclusions. A common technique used for this purpose is the strong parameter estimation method. A stronger version of this technique would involve assessing model parameters independently of their use for prediction. Unfortunately, this more rigorous version is not feasible with standard methods for most processes that are observed in discrete form. Alternatively, the effective parameter estimation method assesses parameter uncertainty through simulations, which can be reliable for specific purposes, such as bounding a system's behavior. However, the issue of determining suitable simulation parameters remains. In this paper, we introduce a simulation-based approach for assessing parameter uncertainty that is more robust and less dependent on discretization, for which we provide statistical confidence and an estimator of simulation parameters. The method is particularly useful for modeling technologies like quantum systems, which typically involve large datasets collected in discrete form. The paper's main concepts and techniques are demonstrated using an example from the quantum technology field. The method described, however, is not limited to this field and can be applied to any area where researchers need to model the behavior of systems using real-valued or categorical data collected in discrete form. The method's effectiveness is shown through a comparison with a more conventional method, and the paper explores its connection to the stronger version of parameter estimation. The approach presented also raises interesting questions and potential applications regarding the use of cross-validation in modeling the behavior of systems over extended periods of time. The paper's final section summarizes the main points, and the appendix contains additional details on a simulation method, a parameter uncertainty estimator, and a confidence estimator. The paper's final section also presents a conclusion, and the appendix contains an expanded discussion on cross-validation. The emergence of Edge Computing is forcing a shift in the computing industry's focus from cloud-centricity to a more decentralized model. This shift creates opportunities for companies to offer cutting-edge solutions closer to users, thus providing faster services and more reliable connectivity. However, providing reliable services at the Edge also calls for a reevaluation of the approach to software development and testing, due to limited resources available at Edge devices, along with the unique performance and security requirements of these environments. This call for reevaluation is being largely overlooked in the literature, which remains dominated by general discussions on Edge Computing, Cloud Computing, and Software-Defined Networking, but lacks targeted discussions on the specific challenges of Edge Computing, particularly in the context of event-driven applications. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by introducing a new testing framework tailored to the unique requirements of Edge Computing, TFE. This event-driven testing framework is comprised of three interdependent components, namely, a parser for identifying relevant events from source codes, a driver for managing the simulation of events, and utilities for executing tests with simulated event data. This event-driven testing framework is then demonstrated through a real-world scenario involving an event-driven IoT application, with the complete implementation of the parser, driver, and utilities available online for reference. This work also contributes a new metric, called the event-driven testing efficiency, which gauges the performance of event-driven testing frameworks like TFE, by evaluating the event-driven testing efficiency of TFE against two alternative testing approaches, namely, traditional unit testing and container-based testing. This research uncovered novel evidence that event-driven testing methods like TFE deliver superior testing efficiency, with results indicating that the event-driven testing efficiency of TFE outperforms the efficiency of traditional unit testing and container-based testing by at least 1.5 times. This breakthrough testing framework like TFE offers companies a chance to identify and fix bugs faster in the development cycle, thus reducing the overall cost of fixing the issue, with the opportunity to explore the theoretical limits of the event-driven testing efficiency of TFE. This study on the event-driven testing efficiency of TFE also raises important questions and hypotheses for the broader software development and testing community to address, along with new research directions and potential solutions to long-standing challenges in software development and testing. This event-driven testing framework like TFE could potentially become a game-changer in the software development and testing industry, with the potential to improve the reliability of software, particularly in the context of event-driven applications, with the opportunity to explore the practical applications of this approach in real-world projects.

A novel approach is proposed for accelerating iterative solvers in time-dependent PDEs by transforming the problem into a form with a stable difference approximation.  The method involves three key steps: first, the original PDE is recast in an explicit form with a finite difference approximation that maintains non-negativity; second, the resulting system of equations is expressed in implicit form; and third, this implicit form is further rearranged to yield a stable difference approximation equivalent to the original PDE.  The proposed method is particularly beneficial for modeling real-world constraints, such as non-negativity, but due to the extra computational cost of the implicit step, it can result in slower convergence when using same-order explicit and implicit solvers.  To address this issue, the paper investigates the use of preconditioned Krylov solvers, such as GMRES, to take advantage of the more accurate implicit step while minimizing the computational cost.  The paper presents numerical results for various PDE applications, including advection, advection-diffusion, Burgers' equation, and a Malthusian model with population dynamics, demonstrating the benefits of preconditioned Krylov solvers for the implicit dimensionless variable difference (IDVD) method.  The results show that the proposed method offers improved accuracy and convergence rates compared to alternative solvers, such as Bi-CGSTAB, for a significant computational cost savings.  The paper also explores the use of IDVD with low-order (Newton) preconditioning for solving nonlinear systems of equations, demonstrating its effectiveness for a range of applications.  The results highlight the potential for the IDVD method to be an efficient and robust solution strategy for a broad class of time-dependent PDEs. Additionally, we found that dusty supernovae can last for about 10 years, which, along with the existing constraints on supernovae rates, could provide a way to use distant dusty supernovae as cosmic distance lamps. For mobile robots to successfully navigate their environment, they require accurate scene flow estimation. This application is critical and demands robust optical flow estimation across arbitrary paths. However, the performance of flow estimation models is often hindered by their reliance on neighbor metrics, particularly cross-channels, which can lead to over-reliance on noisy boundary data and artificial features. This limitation is addressed by modifying the metric learning component of flow estimation models to be unsupervised and only rely on intrinsic properties, thereby preventing the introduction of extrinsic noise from neighbor metrics. However, securing microservices presents unique challenges, primarily stemming from the brief duration of their operations and the difficulty of analyzing their temporal system call patterns. Although techniques like learning temporal rules have shown promise, they are often limited to specific scenarios and require extensive expertise. In contrast, Timeloops utilizes a rule-based learning approach, combining expertise with automated temporal rule generation, to effectively detect security vulnerabilities by leveraging system call patterns over time. This method is particularly well-suited for discovering irregular system call patterns, such as those indicative of QEMU attacks, which manipulate a computer's hardware components to bypass detection by generating normal system call patterns at specific points in time. To demonstrate its utility, Timeloops was applied to creating system call rules for discovering QEMU attacks and generating rules for DoS and injection attacks. Furthermore, this method was incorporated into a protocol for discovering temporal system call patterns in real-time, resulting in the detection of a QEMU attack in a real-world scenario. Deep Learning (DL) has achieved remarkable success in 3D location recognition, with numerous applications in robotics, game simulations, and virtual guides, among others, that rely heavily on accurate place recognition. To date, most popular approaches have been 2D-based, utilizing DELF features for visualization and codebook-based methods such as VGG-SLAM. However, these solutions fall short when faced with complex environments and extensive travel. To overcome these limitations, this research introduces a cutting-edge 3D codebook-based network called AttDLNet, that leverages attention mechanisms and encoder-decoder structures to enhance codebook learning and encode contextual information. By integrating LiDAR scans with contextual information, AttDLNet outperforms state-of-the-art 2D-based methods by 5.21% on the SUN3D dataset, achieving superior performance and greater flexibility. Furthermore, empirical results indicate that AttDLNet's codebooks exhibit increased diversity and distinctiveness, explaining the method's superior location recognition performance. To facilitate codebook learning from raw LiDAR data, the network's architecture includes an encoder-decoder structure, decoding LiDAR scans into codebook entries. To prevent information loss during decoding, a decoder-encoder fusion module is proposed, enabling direct learning of codebook entries from LiDAR scans. Moreover, to enhance codebook learning with contextual information, a cross-encoder is integrated, enabling codebooks to capture contextual details and encode them into codebook entries. The network's codebook learning strategy is evaluated on the SUN3D and CMU Climbing Stairs datasets, with results showing improved codebook diversity and distinctiveness. To validate the method's location recognition performance, AttDLNet is applied to the SUN3D dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art 2D-based methods by 5.21%. The network's flexibility is further demonstrated by successfully recognizing locations on the CMU Climbing Stairs dataset with codebooks learned from the SUN3D dataset.
