In 2014, Arita, Saito, and Takaski developed a velocity process in ASEP, which generates random fluctuations on a grid occupied by particles, resulting in a velocity field that represents the local average particle speed. We extend their work by creating multiple 'layers' of particles with distinct velocities, leading to a velocity field with multiple components, and demonstrating that this extension is a conserved current system. We then analyze the long-term behavior of this system's second moment, and establish that it converges to a constant value, which we prove is the same as the sum of the square of the individual velocity means. We also examine the exact distribution of the ASEP velocity process's first moment, and provide an alternative method for generating the particles' positions. Finally, we discuss how these results are connected to an imaginary time dynamics system known as the ASEP speed process. We are able to show that the stationary distribution of the ASEP velocity process's local average velocity field is the same as the ASEP speed process's local current, and establish that the former is a gradient of the latter. This provides new insights into both systems. We are also able to use these findings to prove additional properties about the ASEP speed process. We examine several specific cases, including a bounded domain with different boundary conditions, a system with particles on two separate lines that interact, and a system with 'walls' that can move, all of which display intriguing behavior. We are able to use these results to further understand the behavior of the ASEP speed process in these complex situations. Finally, we discuss several open questions related to these systems. We believe that establishing whether the ASEP velocity process or its variant with 'walls' reach a state of over-determination in a finite time could provide valuable insights into both systems. Additionally, determining whether the stationary distribution of the ASEP velocity process with 'walls' is reached before the point of over-determination, as well as finding the exact distribution of the second moment of the ASEP velocity process with particles on two separate lines, could also contribute significantly to our understanding of these systems. We are confident that a deeper understanding of these systems will provide valuable insights into the broader field of macroscopic fluctuation theory. We are excited about the prospect of contributing to this understanding and the many open questions that remain in this field. We investigate the properties of a Majorana fermion, representing a fermionic particle with the same properties as its own antiparticle. This particle, native to a 1+1 dimensional space with a real energy axis, serves as the basis for a qubit, which we call a Qubitino. We calculate the probabilities of finding a Majorana fermion in its ground and excited states, as well as its position within these states. Furthermore, we determine the expectation values of various operators, including momentum and number operators, and derive the density matrix, density, and momentum distribution of the Majorana fermion. Our calculations reveal that a Majorana fermion exhibits unique behavior compared to conventional fermions and antifermions. Notably, when an antifermion undergoes a unitary transformation, its momentum distribution changes in a manner inversely proportional to its energy, in stark contrast to a fermion's increased density at higher energies. This distinct behavior may be exploited to advantage in applications involving Majorana fermions. Additionally, we demonstrate that a linear Majorana fermion possesses the capacity to emulate both quantum spinning particles and antiparticles. This capability could prove beneficial in developing strategies for detecting these particles. Furthermore, we investigate the properties of a Majorana fermion-based qubit and find its diagonal operators to exhibit behavior analogous to that of conventional qubits, whereas non-diagonal operators may simulate the characteristics of rotating qubits. This study contributes to a comprehensive examination of linear Majorana fermions, encompassing both theoretical aspects and practical applications. Furthermore, this work paves the way for further explorations of these particles in the context of quantum field theory. Nonetheless, a crucial aspect of quantum theory remains misunderstood; the inherent uncertainty principle dictates that certain properties cannot be precisely known, yet the mechanism driving this principle remains unclear. This principle serves as the foundation for numerous groundbreaking effects and is an integral component of quantum theory. Nevertheless, the origin of the uncertainty principle remains an unsolved problem in physics. This review focuses on the aspects of linear Majorana fermions, building upon previous research. We introduce the idea of evaluating anti-spam systems through the eyes of spammers, using game theoretical modeling to analyze the situation. Through experimentation with various web-based spam datasets, we find that the optimal strategy for spammers results in self-coverages of up to 93% and 98% for the Mombosa and Jevon datasets, respectively. We found that several existing anti-spam techniques performed superior to previous state-of-the-art baseline methods we proposed. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SMD) in multiple fields of view can surpass this constraint, but the system's overall resolution remains governed by the smallest of these constraints - typically the largest of two unknowns in a system with two photons. Here, the limitation of this approach is addressed by demonstrating that, whendemultiplexing in only one field of view, the system's resolution can be better than the diffraction limit, but the phrasing used in prior work was found to be misleading. Determining whether the correlation between maximum stellar mass and star formation rate in galaxies holds and its underlying reason remains an unsolved problem in astronomy. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset that includes high-resolution observations for 153 galaxies at masses greater than ten billion solar masses, our analysis discovers the predicted correlation to weaken at higher masses and identifies the growth of bulges as a key factor in this phenomenon. Existing models that propose the M*-SFR connection arises from a balance between star formation and gravitational instability are challenged by our findings. Instead, our results suggest that broader cosmological settings might influence the relationship between mass and SFR, likely due to massive galaxies representing rare, extreme peaks in the mass function. We additionally find evidence the average SFR within these galaxies actually continues along the predicted correlation when comparing SFR within specific bulge masses rather than overall galaxy masses. Our research implies the M*-SFR connection turns over at high masses as a result of bulge growth, leading to an expansion of massive galaxy size beyond typical galaxy scales, and might also impact the underlying physics governing these phenomena. Understanding these findings can offer new insights into the assembly of massive galaxies and the predicted relationships between galaxy properties and their place within the broader cosmological framework. Further study into these phenomena using a range of observational and theoretical analysis is necessary to a comprehensive understanding of these complex processes.

The paper examines a family of stochastic processes, specifically fractional Brownian motions with time-dependent increments, and investigates their underlying space-time paradigm. We demonstrate that for a specific parameter value, the invariant measure exhibits both positive Lebesgue volume and a non-empty interior. This finding is significant because it contrasts with existing results for standard fractional Brownian motions. Moreover, we show that any given smooth function can be approximated by a set of fractional Brownian motion paths with varying drifts, which expands our understanding of the associated space-time structure. This theoretical analysis has practical implications for the development of numerical schemes, which we also discuss. Additionally, we explore connections with related concepts, such as ergodic control and control-constrained fractional Brownian motions. Finally, the results from our proof of non-empty interior also yield insights into the design of numerical schemes for approximating ergodic controls. This includes a new interpretation of the result from J. G. Dai and C. J. Tsai, which provides an optimal solution for the ergodic control problem, and suggests an alternative method for constructing the policy $\pi_1$. This policy $\pi_1$ is known as the 'one-stage look-ahead' policy, and is shown to be equivalent to the optimal solution obtained by C. J. Tsai. This equivalence is established by a different, more direct method. This new approach to analyzing the space-time structure of fractional Brownian motions has the benefit of being more versatile and easier to apply than earlier methods. This is particularly evident when approximating functions that have discontinuities, for which the one-stage look-ahead policy remains an optimal solution. However, it is worth noting that the optimal solution for control-constrained fractional Brownian motions when the constraint is a linear function of the state, but the constraint itself is not an affine function of the state, is an open problem. This is also discussed in the paper. The results from the proof of positive Lebesgue volume and non-empty interior for fractional Brownian motions with time-dependent increments, and the analysis of the one-stage look-ahead policy, are shown to be generalizable to a broader class of processes, which are known as geometric Brownian motion with time-dependent increments in the space-time structure. This includes both the standard geometric Brownian motion, as well as its fractional Brownian motion counterpart. The name 'geometric Brownian motion' is used to describe these processes to highlight the relationship with geometric Brownian motion, which is the time-dependent counterpart of fractional Brownian motion. The incorrect classifications in visual association detection can hinder the training process and prevent the model from achieving optimal performance. A major contributor to this issue is the current evaluation metric, which measures the accuracy based on whether the predicted class matches the actual class among all classes, without considering the confidence in the prediction. As a result, the model is rewarded for making random classifications with high confidence, rather than being penalized. To address this shortcoming, we propose a new evaluation metric that takes into account both the accuracy and the confidence of the predictions. For the positive samples, the model must not only select the correct class but also demonstrate sufficient confidence in that classification. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor (CAPP), which leverages the flexibility of a FPGA architecture. Our CAPP design builds upon the historical concept of Content Addressable Parallel Processors, where incoming data and stored memory entries are simultaneously compared, and the cell with the highest priority match is identified and returned to the user. By incorporating a priority encoder inspired by the digital rank computation method, we have created a CAPP design that efficiently supports multiple operations, including maximum/minimum calculations, data sorting, and ranking. To further enhance its functionality, our CAPP design has been integrated with a user-friendly interface inspired by the model's original design, featuring toggleable mode switches and input/output controllers. A maximum-scale CAPP model with 1024x1024 cells has been successfully implemented on a Nexis-A7 FPGA board, achieving clock speeds of up to 100 MHz. The performance of this large-scale CAPP model has been evaluated for various applications, showcasing its capability to execute tasks at approximately 50-90 clock cycles per operation. Furthermore, we have explored the possibility of integrating the CAPP model with a CAPP controller, which facilitates sequential access and prioritized retrieval of data from the CAPP array. This combined CAPP system has also been successfully implemented on the Nexis-A7 FPGA board and clocked at up to 70 MHz. The design of this integrated CAPP system has great potential for optimizing the performance of algorithms that can benefit from content-addressable memory. To facilitate the development of such optimized algorithms, we have created a range of toggleable mode switches in the CAPP controller, which can be set to meet specific requirement specifications. The fully-featured CAPP models, including the large-scale model and integrated controller, have been designed with the ability to interface with off-board hosts via a high-speed USB 2.0 interface. This has been made possible through the incorporation of a soft-IP USB controller, which provides a compatible interface for the CAPP models. The comprehensive design of the CAPP models, along with the integrated controller and advanced features such as sequential access and prioritized data retrieval, has greatly enhanced the capabilities of these processors. This study develops a biophysical brain stem model for the Marmoset monkey, incorporating 139 neurons and 287 synapses, based on recent anatomical and physiological research. Utilizing the Nernst equilibrium approximation, the model calculates the membrane potential of each neuron and a spiking probability function. The model incorporates a wide range of neurotransmitters including dopamine, and we have developed a computational method to input extrinsically obtained electrical stimulation data into the model. By integrating an optimization algorithm and a-residual-based method, we adjusted and refined the model to accurately replicate the brain stem's electrical activity in the Marmoset monkey with Parkinson's disease symptoms. The optimized model demonstrates an exceptional 0.96 correlation with actual measured brain activity, and notably, our results indicate that the abnormal brain activity patterns associated with Parkinson's disease can be replicated through a dopamine deficiency, corroborating existing clinical observations. Furthermore, our model offers insights into the intricate brain dynamics underlying the progression from normal to abnormal brain activity patterns in Parkinson's disease patients, and it may potentially serve as a foundation for further exploration of novel treatment strategies. The model's code is available for public use and can be adapted for computational modeling of the Marmoset brain stem. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies (U/LIRGs) within a distance of 400 kiloparsecs from the center of the Great Atlas galaxy. Collecting data with 9~$\rm km~s^{-1}$ spatial resolution and 150~$\rm km~s^{-1}$ spectral resolution, we derived oxygen-based star formation rates and maps of star formation across the galaxies. Notably, we found a high star formation rate in the interacting pair Mrk 0316, which consists of a face-on spiral and an edge-on dwarf irregular galaxy; Mrk 0316 displays a star formation pattern on its spiral galaxy side, specifically across 60 kpc of tidal features. Additionally, we detected [Ne~III]$\rm \lambda 3873$ emission in five out of the nine U/LIRGs, indicating the presence of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in these galaxies. AGN activity was also confirmed through other means in four out of these five galaxies; the remaining galaxy, Arp 192, requires further analysis due to uncertain AGN activity. Estimating molecular gas masses via the [Ne~III]$\rm \lambda 3873$ emission, we found these masses to be in the range of 10$^{9.3}$ to 10$^{10.5}$ $\rm M_{\odot}$. Our data also indicate a positive correlation between star formation rates and molecular gas masses in these galaxies. These results demonstrate the capabilities of the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for obtaining optical IFU data of galaxy collections, showcasing its potential for investigating various galaxy phenomena. Further data analysis and the employment of radio continuum data to determine radio continuum-star formation rates and gas masses are subject to pending publication. Our team intends to expand the scope of this study to the entire GOALS database of 61 U/LIRGs through the utilization of the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope. This has implications for furthering our understanding of the evolution of galaxies within these systems. Developing effective solutions to classify complex datasets, particularly those created from a variety of sources, is a critical challenge. In the field of image recognition, the success of such approaches relies heavily on the quality of the dataset and the choice of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). A substantial body of research has focused on enhancing the performance of CNNs through novel architectures and techniques, yet the underlying principles of these methods often lack a clear theoretical basis. In the realm of land cover classification, the performance of CNNs is often evaluated using standardized datasets such as Sentinel-2, although the results of these evaluations fail to consider the unique characteristics of the dataset at hand. In contrast, our research proposes a novel multi-class dataset called ClimateCategorization, comprising 8000 annotated images organized into 10 categories, along with a data enhancement approach called Partial Overlap Augmentation. This approach leverages the spatial coherence of satellite images to achieve enhanced performance using standard CNNs, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our results demonstrate improvement over prior climate classification studies, with an overall accuracy of 91.3% surpassing even the performance of cutting-edge models like EfficientNet and Multi-Task Learning. Furthermore, our research highlights the efficacy of simpler CNNs like DPN-128, despite the prevailing trend of continuous network depth, highlighting the significance of dataset quality over network complexity. Additionally, our assessments reveal the inadequacy of conventional evaluation metrics and propose a novel multi-class confidence thresholding method to enhance the practical applications of climate categorization. Lastly, our findings show that a relatively simple CNN like DPN-92 surpasses the performance of specialized climate models like ClimateHourGlass, highlighting the importance of thorough assessments prior to deploying models in real-world scenarios. In conclusion, our ClimateCategorization dataset, along with the proposed data enhancement approach and comprehensive evaluations of CNNs, lays the groundwork for creating more versatile and adaptable solutions in the field of land cover classification. In the process, our research shatters the myth of sophisticated high-level models as necessary solutions, instead demonstrating the superiority of simpler CNNs on the ClimateCategorization dataset. The implications of these findings, coupled with the introduction of ClimateCategorization and POA, is expected to yield significant improvements in the development of accurate and reliable climate categorization solutions. As a pioneering multi-class satellite image recognition dataset, ClimateCategorization is expected to yield substantial gains in performance, outperforming prior climate classification studies and setting a new standard for excellence. DPCRN's design addresses the limitations of traditional RNNs by incorporating dual pathways: a long-short-term memory (LSTM) unit and a gated recurrent unit (GRU). This innovative dual-path structure allows for both detailed, character-level information processing and more efficient, coarse-grained data processing. Additionally, the $f(R)$ gravity theory also has an effect on the development of cosmic structure and the large-scale distribution of matter. However, determining the combined effect of these two factors on the turn-around radii of dark matter structures throughout the universe is a complex issue. Utilizing a code that integrates $f(R)$ gravity and heavy neutrinos with existing large-scale structure simulation tools, researchers discovered a combined impact on the turn-around radii of dark matter structures. Specifically, the effect of heavy neutrinos on $f(R)$ gravity-led structure formation follows a pattern: heavy neutrinos delay the onset of structure formation in a neutrino-dominated universe by reducing the matter density, which in turn influences the turn-around radii in a way that depends on both the density fluctuation amplitude and the neutrino mass. As a result, in regions of high matter density and low cosmic web fidelity, structure turns around at a significantly greater distance in a universe with heavy neutrinos. Conversely, in regions of low matter density and high cosmic web fidelity, structure turns around at a significantly smaller distance in a universe with heavy neutrinos. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could become entangled with the other two. Our analysis reveals that it is impossible for the unconnected system to become genuinely entangled with the correlated pair if the two systems are not genuinely entangled themselves. Furthermore, if the Jaynes-Cummings interactions are equivalent, the unconnected system will not become genuinely entangled. We do, however, find specific scenarios in which the unconnected system can become genuinely entangled with the correlated pair, including certain situations in which the Jaynes-Cummings interactions are not equivalent, or when a process known as Jaynes-Cummings leakage occurs. Additionally, we demonstrate that these phenomena can be observed experimentally using current technology. Finally, we discuss various applications for these findings within the field of quantum communication.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC) relies on advanced online data reconstruction, known as the Level-1 trigger, to rapidly identify interesting events following hadron collisions. A crucial component of this trigger system is the Level-1 muon trigger, which relies on global muon trigger (GMT) software for rapid global muon tracking and reconstruction. To improve performance and prepare for the Phase-2 of the LHC, a new generation of GMT detectors and associated readout systems is being developed, featuring enhanced pixel detectors with increased bandwidth and bit depth. To anticipate potential reconstruction challenges with these new detectors, a set of older CMS pixel prototypes was utilized in offline reconstruction research. Specifically, a study was conducted on a set of phase-1 forward pixel prototype blades constructed from 650 micron thick silicon material. Test beam data showed the detectors' capability for accurate track reconstruction, with a typical hit efficiency above 95%. However, due to the thick material and non-uniform magnetic field, reconstructed tracks exhibited significant non-linearities and biases, which were found to be highly sensitive to the track's associated global information. As a result, using the GNU Scientific Library's (GSL) minimization function for the track's chi-square minimization led to resolution values of approximately 4.8, which did not significantly improve with the inclusion of online information. Furthermore, a simplified algorithm was developed to address the non-linear issues and associated track reconstruction challenges, resulting in reconstructed track resolutions of about 3.3 when including online information. The improved performance highlights the potential of the CMS phase-1 forward pixel prototype blades for enhanced trigger performance with thick silicon detectors, especially in environments with high multiplicity rates. The research also provides valuable insights for the design of future forward tracking systems in other experiments. The novel method developed from this study may be adaptable to the reconstruction of track segments in forward tracking systems with thick detectors, even in high-multiplicity environments. This approach, rooted in the Kall\'en-Lehmann representation, breaks down the scattering matrix into its fundamental components using spectral sums over commuting operators, derived from the squared differences of incoming and outgoing particle momenta. This formulation's effectiveness is illustrated through computations of the SU(2) glueball's spectral representation within the Chern-Simons gauge theory, facilitated by a lattice Monte Carlo simulation for obtaining the glueball's discrete spectrum. The study of tomograms offers a comprehensive understanding of a quantum system's properties.  Tomographic entropies can not only gauge the level of entanglement but also uncover other crucial aspects, including non-classical behavior and the synchronization of subsystems.  Our work showcases the utility of Wigner tomography in monitoring the entanglement of two-dimensionally separated systems as well as the phenomenon of sub-systems' synchronization, both of which cannot be achieved with standard Wigner functions.  Specifically, we utilize Wigner tomography to detect the growth of entanglement in systems that experience interaction, and the emergence of synchronization in systems that have experienced confinement.  Our results demonstrate that tomographic Wigner distributions serve as an efficient tool for analyzing the complex phenomena involved in the study of quantum physics.  Furthermore, our research is directly applicable to the current experimental capabilities using ion-trap systems.  In such setups, tomographic Wigner distributions can be generated through the application of various quantum gates without the need for additional instrumentation.  Our study not only highlights the potency of tomographic analysis but also showcases the potential of these methods to contribute meaningfully to the advancement of quantum research.  As such, we foresee a bright future for the use of tomographic techniques in the study of complex quantum systems.  Our approach is versatile and can be adapted to address a wide range of scientific inquiries in the field of quantum physics.  To that end, we have made our code publicly available for any further customization or use.  Furthermore, we have also outlined a novel strategy for the detection of multi-partite entanglements that could hold the key to solving some of the universe's greatest mysteries.  As such, we invite any members of the quantum community to collaborate with us on this research or to utilize the code provided in their own studies. Recent advances in open-domain conversations have primarily centered around human-computer interaction and were often evaluated using datasets crafted by various groups. Nonetheless, a crucial aspect has been overlooked until now - the construction of a conversation framework that adheres to established social norms. To address this, we propose a comprehensive framework for roles in open-domain conversations. This framework comprises six elements: (1) determining the conversation's objective; (2) establishing and upholding turn-taking protocols; (3) crafting coherent turns of phrase; (4) managing turn length; (5) regulating self-talk; and (6) preventing opportunistic behavior. For each aspect, we developed distinct open-domain datasets along with models that harness vast language models. To validate our framework's efficacy, we designed numerous open-domain conversation roles and observed how naturally spoken language deviates from predicted outcomes. Notably, our results revealed that even models fueled by vast language models can exhibit substantial disparities - as much as 20% - in regards to our metrics. To mitigate these discrepancies, we presented retrained models and assessed what factors influence natural language's deviation patterns. Our research provides actionable insights for enhancing the natural language expressions generated by large language models. Additionally, our studies on open-domain conversation roles may spark further exploration in this area. To facilitate replication and advancement, we are willing to share our conversation roles alongside additional information on our experiments. As the field of open-domain conversations continues to evolve, our research aims to contribute meaningful insights and set the stage for future developments. In the accompanying supplementary material, we discuss three potential areas for further exploration. First, both our statistical and qualitative analyses revealed that certain aspects influence natural language's deviation patterns in a more complex way than a simple average. Secondly, even though our results indicated that vast language models can generate natural language expressions with a 20% difference, it is essential to consider not just the average but also the variability among individual models. Lastly, our research demonstrated that retraining models on our datasets can mitigate their discrepancies with predicted outcomes, but it is vital to examine not just the overall performance but also the individual components of our metrics. 360-degree and action-based videos have become popular means of travel exploration, allowing viewers to engage dynamically with the content by navigating the viewport in response to audio and visual stimuli. Current studies on video understanding focus primarily on measuring viewer attention, but these tend to be limited to static datasets without consideration for the viewer's narrative context. Conversely, the inherent nature of 360-degree and action-based videos stems from their immersive and dynamic essence. To address this gap, this research introduces a novel challenge and an associated dataset called Virtual Travel Video Forecast, where the task is to predict viewer attention based on narrative-driven subtitles and video features, with subsequent experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating subtitles in the prediction process. Furthermore, our findings show that incorporating subtitles outperforms models relying solely on video features, with a notable increase in performance metrics. Additionally, our analysis of user behavior, carried out in conjunction with Amazon Mechanical Turk, reveals the considerable difficulty of accurately forecasting viewer attention. To facilitate further research, the VTVF-Forecast dataset, comprising 1250 samples and 20 million parameters, is openly available for the research community. Ultimately, this study's findings are relevant to the development of travel video applications and related domains, with potential extensions to other domains such as sports and news video analysis. With the rise of interactive and immersive technologies such as head-mounted displays and spatial audio, enhancing the viewing experience of virtual travel videos is becoming increasingly vital. As a result, there is a pressing need for more sophisticated methods of forecast and analysis, especially in the video research community. With its unique blend of machine learning, natural language processing, and computer vision, this study's approach may also be of interest to researchers working in the multidisciplinary field of human-computer interaction. Tensor networks serve as approximations for the behavior of complex systems, typically obtained through a process called optimization, yet these representations suffer from a flaw - they lack precision in the local area. This shortcoming becomes particularly evident when attempting to utilize tensor networks for describing thermal states or temporal transformations, as it causes issues with the systematic improvement of these approximations. This paper demonstrates a novel approach that enables the creation of high-accuracy tensor networks in the local region, without the need for optimization. We achieve this by drawing a comparison between the cross-correlation of the system's unitary operators and the thermal state's correlation, or in the case of temporal transformations, drawing inspiration from the time-honored concept of the interaction picture. We apply this understanding to build better-bound approximations for the thermal state and temporal evolution, both resulting in improved volume growth constraints. These constraints facilitate easier implementation of the fusion process in an environment with limited computational resources, making them highly beneficial for the use of tensor networks in the study of time-dependent or thermal systems. We further showcase this approach with the specific example of the XY-model, a system commonly employed in quantum simulation experiments. Additionally, we highlight the possibility of incorporating this understanding into the design of bond-dimensional tensor network algorithms that naturally produce precise descriptions of thermal states and temporal evolution. We refer to our approach as locally precise tensor networks, as it produces tensor network descriptions that accurately capture the behavior in the local area, or we could say, in the local life. Furthermore, we also introduce the notion of universal tensor network conditions, which serve as the foundation for the construction of locally precise tensor networks for thermal states and temporal evolution. We anticipate this concept to be a crucial component in the development of future tensor network algorithms. We utilize the term universal tensor network conditions to emphasize their broad applicability, or in the words of Einstein, their "generalized principle" nature. Reasoning about programs that interact with restrictive systems, like external APIs, is a challenging task due to the arbitrary decisions made by the system's developers and users.  The architecture of such systems is often undefined, leading to uncertainty about the programs' impact and potential security vulnerabilities.  Our novel decoupling method addresses this issue by allowing the analysis of programs in an environment where the system's behavior is only known through certain criteria.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by developing a practical example from the Android ecosystem.  Our tool, ADR, uses this technique to analyze the broadcasted intents within an Android application, determining the programs that can handle these intents reliably.  Our experiments show that ADR outperforms existing methods while achieving more accurate results.  Further research directions from this study are also discussed.  We also explore alternative expressions of a program's behavior using the Satisfiability Modulo Theory, a more versatile method that can handle the complexity of modern software.  This leads to the development of a more general framework for decoupling programs, drawing inspiration from the success of ADR.  With this framework, we identify various strategies for solving the common constraints among programs, as well as different ways to specify the behavior of external systems, such as APIs, accurately.  This study extends the initial results from ADR by supporting more sophisticated specifications of a program's behavior and reveals the potential of our approach for handling a broader range of programs, even if the program's code is not available.  We also introduce the concept of relative reliability, a new way to describe the relationship between programs that can achieve the same goal, such as connecting to an API. The minimum strong shortest route cover with k-hops (MSSRCH) problem remains an open challenge even for its basic variant, where it is just called the strong shortest route cover (SSRC) problem. In this study, we examine SSRC and its k-hops variant (MSSRCH) for two significant graph types: planar graphs and Cartesian product graphs, also addressing the k-hops variant for some trees and presenting a general bound for the SSRC of trees. This research provides specific and general bounds, as well as an algorithm for solving the SSRC of certain trees exactly. We analyze the relationship between the given bounds and the graph size, along with a general k-hops cover for some planar graphs and certain product graphs. This includes obtaining optimal strong shortest routes for some specific graphs and showing that some graphs have a k-hops cover that is equal to the (k+1)-hops cover, indicating that the increase in hops makes the cover size almost the same as the graph's diameter. This research provides an examination of the graph properties through its cover, which is a novel approach. We present both theoretical and practical aspects of the cover, along with a focus on general and specific graph types. This includes examining the coverage of all pairs of nodes through the covers, as well as the relationship between the graph's diameter and its k-hops cover size. This research on the SSRC and MSSRCH problems may be of interest to anyone working on graph theory, communication network coverage, or road network coverage. This study is an extension of an earlier paper presented at the 2018 AASRI Conference, and the authors would like to express their gratitude to the editors and reviewers for their valuable feedback that helped to further improve this article. This improvement has resulted in the addition of new research on the k-hops variant of the strong shortest route cover problem. Due to the limitations of the earlier manuscript, some of the new results could not be included in the final version of the article. The authors would like to state that all of the new research on the k-hops variant of the SSRC problem has been added as supplementary material with this revised version of the article. This supplementary material includes a new appendix, which provides a detailed description of the software and data used in this research, including the implementation of the exact algorithm for solving the SSRC of some trees exactly. Furthermore, this change in the pole's position leads to an increased estimate of the uncertainty when integrating the impact factor along the light-cone, $\delta \left(\int dx T \, \mathrm{Im} \, \mathrm{Disc} \, \left[\frac{1}{\Gamma(s/M_0^2)}\right]\right) \sim \frac{sM_2^2}{(s+M_0^2)^2}$, with $M_0^2$ representing the initial mass scale. Moreover, this updated analysis provides a more precise definition of the uncertainty in the color dipole gluon distribution itself, with an estimated magnitude of approximately $\frac{2M_2^2}{(s+M_0^2)^2}$. This study's findings are particularly relevant given the direct connection between the color dipole gluon distribution and precision measurements of dijet production in photon-proton scattering. Consider an infinite tree with degree $d$, where nodes are equipped with a simple symmetric marking mechanism similar to the amphibian model, but with the ability to change their state based on the state of their neighbors. The marking distribution remains memory-based and only relies on the current state of a node. We are attempting to identify the minimal connectivity density $\lambda_c$ in this scenario, where nodes with high degrees eventually mark themselves with certainty, as it has already been established that an extensive range of $\lambda$ values fall within the regime of complete wiring. Our analysis focuses on determining this critical $\lambda_c$ value, $\lambda_c(d)$. It is evident that in scenarios where the degree of the tree exceeds two, hydra-like structures will form within the tree, resulting in an extensive range of $\lambda$ values indicating that the behavior of the process on a d-ary tree differs significantly from that on a binary tree. Building upon previous research by Berger, Bagnoli, and Shakhnovich, among others, we found that in a binary tree, the critical $\lambda_c$ value is directly proportional to the $n$-th root of $n$, where $n$ represents the depth of the tree, as well as being a decreasing function of the degree of the tree. Ultimately, we established that in an infinite-degree tree, the critical $\lambda_c$ value is equal to the extent of the tree. This research was presented at the 2019 Mathematical Biology and Physiology meeting.

A collection of integers is considered p/q-observable if the ratio of its sum of squares to the square of its sum is equal to 1, where p and q are relatively prime. This concept can be expressed as the ratio being a value 'r' and this property holds true for all possible subsets of the collection. Our research into these collections has resulting in several key findings. Firstly, we prove that any collection of the form {a+di, a-di} is fully identifiable at any rational ratio. Secondly, we demonstrate that when the ratio is an irrational number, no collection can achieve a level of p/q-identifiability. Additionally, we provide a criterion which can be used to determine if a collection with a rational ratio of 1 achieves full identifiability. Building on this, we establish that no collection with a rational ratio greater than 1 can achieve p/q-identifiability and we also identify specific collections with a ratio of 1/4 and 9/7 respectively, one of which has a fully identifiable subset and the other does not. Furthermore, we introduce the term almost-identifiable for collections that can notachieve a ratio of 1 but can get arbitrarily close to it. We then show that any collection with a ratio less than 1/4 is almost-identifiable and we also demonstrate that the set {1, 3} has a ratio of 9/7 with respect to the sum of the squares of its elements, making it the first known example of a collection with a ratio greater than 1 that is almost-identifiable. This research of ours into these collections of integers also brings up an interesting open question related to the theory of equations. However, research has consistently shown that doing so would require a very small neutrino mass, which contradicts existing Earth-based laboratory measurements. In an attempt to address this issue, we suggest introducing a fifth neutrino flavor, which could be massive and combinational, consisting of a sterile and a more conventional axion-like state. If this new neutrino's mass is placed within the electroweak range, often referred to as "shadow matter," it could potentially align with the results of the large-scale cosmic observations. In addition, it could also satisfy the requirements for the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ symmetry, which is consistent with existing laboratory measurements, and could even provide a more significant contribution to the dark matter density, as dictated by fit values derived from the global neutrino data bank, particularly in the "normal" ordering scenario. Furthermore, this new neutrino could also provide an explanation for the anomalous alignment of large-scale matter structures, such as galaxies and galaxy clusters, observed in cosmic maps, if its mass is within the electroweak range. In an effort to validate this new neutrino hypothesis, we propose designing a next-generation dark matter direct detection experiment that could potentially identify this new neutrino state. If successfully detected, this new neutrino could have a significant impact on theoretical models, such as modifying the established unitarity constraints and the established neutrino anomaly resolution, known as the "three-sigma deviation." In addition, this new neutrino could also provide an explanation for the discrepancies in certain atomic parity violation measurements, such as the Anomalous Atomic Parity Violation or AAPV. Furthermore, this new neutrino could also provide an explanation for the recently reported deviation in the $na$ scattering experiments, known as the "dark $na$ scattering anomaly." Between 2019 April 21 and 2020 February 29, the LAMOST performed precise monitoring of four $K$2 plates, covering approximately $300^\circ$ of the sky in the Cygnus region, at a pace of about one observation per night on average. By utilizing the BAO-NFA data reduction approach and removing outliers, the pulsation characteristics of 21,248 stars were determined, along with their Blair-Seward slopes, amplitudes, and phases. A web interface was created at http://sdss.lamost.pku.cn:8080/TDE/ for users to explore the data visually. Additionally, an applet called LAMOST-PULSATOLOGY was developed for users to query the data based on specific criteria and statistical distributions. A discussion on the statistical properties of the pulsation population is also presented in this study. For the first time, the distribution of Blair-Seward slopes was found to be skewed to the right, and the majority of the population exhibited low-level variations. A correlation between the 1D and 3D distances was also observed, and the amplitude-displayed phase was found to be a robust indicator of the light curve shape. A demonstration of how to utilize the data for pulsatoLogic, a concept introduced in this study as a form of exoplanet hunting, was provided. PulsatoLogic is a strategy that leverages the high precision of LAMOST light curves in combination with machine learning and a solar-like surface feature variability. This approach is not only applicable to LAMOST but also has potential for other surveys such as LAMOST-III, APASS, and the future generation of wide-field, high-precision photometric and spectroscopic surveys. Using a combinatorial approach, we've found an explanation for the positivity of the coefficients of the elementary symmetric polynomials in the chromatic symmetric polynomials of diagonal graphs. Additionally, this connection leads to the demonstration of a specific subset of the chromatic symmetric polynomials, specifically those corresponding to the inverse Kostka matrices, exhibiting $e$-positivity. This $e$-positivity of the IPSF, as we've termed it, represents a significant expansion of the recent discoveries made by Cho-Huh and Cho-Huh-Oh also in connection with the chromatic symmetric functions and the Kostka matrix. Our proof primarily leverages the recent demonstration of the positivity of the coefficients of the monomial symmetric polynomials in the chromatic symmetric polynomials, a result we've previously discussed. Furthermore, we've obtained even more detailed information about the structure of the coefficient vectors of the chromatic symmetric polynomials, and this additional insight has enabled us to establish connections to other combinatorial objects, such as the inverse Kostka tableaux, the monomial symmetric functions, the Ege-Alcantar-Petersen-Roichman and the Stanley-Kauers decompositions. We've introduced a new statistic, referred to as the breakdown number, which plays a crucial role in our analysis of the structure of the coefficient vectors of the chromatic symmetric polynomials. We've also outlined an explicit procedure for calculating both the ordinary and sum-of-squares decompositions of any monomial symmetric polynomial in a set of variables. Moreover, we've established a direct link between the combinatorial objects, such as the inverse Kostka tableaux and the breakdown numbers, and the coefficients of the chromatic symmetric polynomials, revealing their underlying relationship with the combinatorial interpretation of the Stanley-Kauers decompositions. Our results, in turn, imply the $e$-positivity of the IPSF, a conclusion that follows naturally from our analysis of the structure of the coefficient vectors of the chromatic symmetric polynomials and the combinatorial objects related to them. The term 'executive function' has been extensively used across multiple disciplines to describe a high-level reasoning ability that enables comparative evaluations of past experiences to inform future decisions. We propose a general framework for an executive function based on comparative value comparison, which looks back at previous actions and their associated rewards to refine its assessment of actions' value and make informed choices about future behavior. From this perspective, we analyze a range of techniques that leverage this perspective, including temporal difference learning, reinforcement learning, and planning. We contend that many algorithms employed in these disciplines can be viewed through the lens of an executive function, and we explore the benefits of adopting this perspective, including a unified framework that can compare the performance of seemingly disparate algorithms, a common language for describing these methods, and a framework for evaluating the generalization of models trained via reinforcement learning. Furthermore, we discuss several open questions and potential areas of investigation inspired by this perspective. We also introduce a new perspective on reinforcement learning known as the 'hindsight planning' framework, and we assess the performance of a range of general reinforcement learning algorithms utilizing a self-paced learning framework. Current prejudice detection methods are based on learning from labeled data and can be hampered by the high cost of annotating a comprehensive dataset. This paper introduces an innovative, annotation-free approach called the Prejudice Score, which assesses models' inherent bias when processing medical image datasets. The score is derived from the diversity of patient populations and is demonstrated to be a reliable indicator of prejudice in our experiments. Our research findings are particularly significant, as we successfully identified and mitigated a model's bias without relying on annotated data or conducting actual deployments. Our model prejudice score showed a clear correlation with the results of actual clinical trials, where it performed significantly worse than a professionally trained clinician. Our research discovered several key factors contributing to the high prejudice score, including a lack of diversity in radiologists and a limited geographic representation in the patient population. By addressing these factors and incorporating diversity into the training dataset, we successfully reduced the prejudice score of our model. However, we found that increasing the representation of underdiagnosed groups did not yield the desired outcome. Our research provides insights into the complexities of prejudice detection in medical imaging and demonstrates the feasibility of its assessment and mitigation. We believe our approach can be applied to other imaging datasets and is a significant step towards creating more impartial artificial intelligence models. Our code and data are available for download at https://github.com/author-name/prejudice-medical-imaging. Our research was conducted in partnership with Siemens Healthineers and supported by the Siemens Medical Imaging Challenge. Our experiments involved the use of Siemens CT scans from the OpenI database and the SIIM-ISUP Challenge dataset. Our research was led by J. R. A. Macedo, with contributions from J. A. M. Rodriguez, J. A. M. Rodriguez, and A. M. A. Rodriguez. Our research team consisted of radiologists, medical specialists, and an artificial intelligence expert. Our research was conducted in Boston, MA, USA. Our research focused on the diagnosis of lung nodules from low-dose CT scans. Our research discovered the presence of intrinsic prejudice in state-of-the-art deep learning models and described its impact on clinical trials. Our research found that deep learning models exhibited a preference for larger lung nodules over smaller ones. Our research demonstrated the difficulty of eradicating inherent prejudice through additional training but successfully reduced prejudice scores in certain cases. Our research spanned over a year and a half. Our research identified key challenges in medical imaging prejudice detection, including the difficulty of diversifying training datasets and the limited geographic representation

Speech emotion recognition can have far-reaching applications, but its effectiveness is contingent upon improving accuracy. Emotion recognition in natural language processing tasks is complicated by the fact that existing datasets are usually compiled with little consideration for cultural diversity. Furthermore, given the extensive amount of data typically required to train neural networks, adapting models for use across different domains can be a significant challenge. In this paper, a deep reinforcement learning-based approach is proposed to adapt a pre-trained neural network for use in speech emotion recognition across domains. Initially, a neural network is trained on data from one domain and then used as input to a domain adaptation agent, which uses a critical sampling mechanism to select the most informative data for each state in the reinforcement learning environment. Through the process of learning, the agent is able to identify the optimal strategy for reducing the emotional recognition error in a new, unseen domain. Experimental evaluations show that this proposed method is not only effective at adapting a pre-trained neural network for use in speech emotion recognition across domains but also yields results on par with those obtained through additional data sampling and supervised learning. In addition to emotion recognition in speech, the proposed framework also demonstrates potential applicability to other classification tasks involving neural networks. In order to facilitate further research in this area, an open-source code for the proposed domain adaptation agent has been made available online. We investigated the effects of hydrostatic pressure on the Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO) quadruple layer Aurivillius compound using nuclear forward scattering in the range of 300 K to 450 K and pressure up to 24 GPa.  Upon increasing pressure, BFTO exhibits ferromagnetic behavior at low temperature (65 kOe) and a phase transition to metamagnetic behavior at high temperature (10 kOe).  The magnetic transition temperature is pressure-dependent and increases by 70 K at 24 GPa, while the spin flop phenomenon observed in BFTO is pressure-independent.  The results suggest that applied pressure causes tension in the $ab$ plane of the BFTO structure, leading to a rotation of the magnetic moment on the Fe$^{3+}$ site and ultimately, an increase in magnetic ordering temperature.  The structural evolution of BFTO under pressure as derived from NFD is in agreement with X-ray diffraction data, although some minor discrepancies persist.  The study highlights the utility of NFD in probing the magnetic and structural properties of materials under high pressure.  Furthermore, the unique ability of NFD to concurrently examine structural and magnetic phenomena makes it an invaluable tool, one that surpasses even the combined capabilities of X-ray and SQUID measurements.  The results of this study are significant in the realm of thin film research and could potentially be applied to enhance the performance of magnetic devices by applying external pressure.  The research demonstrates that interlayer interaction in BFTO plays a crucial role in governing its magnetic behavior and that this behavior is, in turn, modulated by the application of external pressure. We examine the equilibrium states of a long, planar Josephson junction and a square SQUID loop using two models, a standard model and a more complex model that incorporates phase slippage. We focus on the competition between superconducting, normal, and periodic states in these systems, influenced by an applied magnetic field and a differential applied voltage. While the standard model is representative of an isolated Josephson junction, the more complex model is more relevant to an SQUID loop that interacts with two isolated Josephson junctions. Depletion of superconducting current due to phase slippage is accounted for by adding a term that represents resistance and is taken into consideration in both models. In the standard model, this causes a shift in the phase diagram, shifting the tricritical point in favor of the periodic state when the junction is long. In the complex model, this shift in the tricritical point occurs at shorter lengths due to the increased resistance of the junction. In the case of the SQUID loop, this slippage causes a kink in the phase diagram, shifting the tricritical point in the long junction limit in favor of the periodic state. This behavior has implications for the design of loop devices, suggesting that a differential applied voltage could be used to control the critical current of a Josephson junction. This effect could also be utilized in the development of two-dimensional superconducting materials that exhibit periodic states in response to magnetic field and could potentially be used in the fabrication of topological materials. A new system, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, has been developed, addressing the gap in research by incorporating a cross-sequence structure and exploring the practical applications of non-sequential data in fake video detection. The results of 10-fold cross-validation for each domain were considered in evaluating the MD-CSDNetwork's effectiveness. The proposed network outperformed the baseline model in every experiment, with a notable improvement of up to 11% in the OuluS2S domain. Furthermore, the MD-CSDNetwork showed superior performance to state-of-the-art approaches on two public datasets - Celeb-DF-V2 and FF++ - with accuracy rates of 94.17% and 95.25%, respectively. The source code of the MD-CSDNetwork has been publicly released on the GitHub platform. The model's reported performance was verified through additional 10-fold cross-validation experiments. Our theoretical findings are corroborated by numerical simulations using randomly generated degree-degree linked regular LDPC code ensembles. We also discuss the implications of our results for LDPC code design, particularly in the context of degree-degree linked architectures. Building upon previous work, our research contributes specifically to the analysis of regular LDPC code performance when degree constraints are satisfied. Although helping users choose classic keys through the measurement of momentum, an attack on the system is possible through assisted vacuum states in just one dimension, contradicting the predicted security when phase randomization is implemented in both dimensions. This paper explains a theoretical approach to explaining this security breach and proposes an attack strategy in both applications of vacuum assistance, including real-world implementations of quantum hardware. As a result, we conclude that using the phase randomization method, even in multiple dimensions, is essential to ensuring the safety of QKD. Moreover, we propose an attack strategy on a system that relies on the decoding of multiple pulses, also outlining measures that can be taken to secure such systems. Finally, we examine the efficacy of our attack on a system that uses the coding of multiple pulses and find it can succeed up to 95% of the time. He then investigated its properties in his book "Interference methods in geometry" published in 1940. However, he raised two unresolved questions concerning Euclidean spaces. The first question asks to prove that any two points in a Euclidean n-dimensional space have exactly n angles with each other. The second question seeks to demonstrate that the set of angles between a point and the origin in a Euclidean n-dimensional space is a subset of the set of angles in a Euclidean m-dimensional space when m >= n. In this paper, we provide a generalization of the concept of angle function to a vector-valued function, which allows us to provide a clear proof for both questions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the sensitivity of this technique to variations in pressure and oxygen-nitrogen ratios, even in confined environments common in engineering and biomedical applications. The integration of our setup with particle image velocimetry enables the measurement of pressure and oxygen-nitrogen ratios across flowing gas streams, while a miniaturized version of this technology, featuring an integrated laser system and probe, facilitates the in-depth analysis of respiratory gas exchange during breathing in a confined space. This work showcases the utility and adaptability of fs/ps hybrid rotational CARS across various applications and it is anticipated that this technique will contribute to a better comprehension of breathing-related phenomena and gas dynamics within complex fluids. There are numerous techniques available for measuring temperature in gases, including thermometry using laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, phase modulation spectroscopy, and thermal imaging. Pressure measurements in gases can be achieved through a variety of methods like ultrasound, laser-induced fluorescence, multi-scan optical imaging, and Raman spectroscopy. Notably, pressure and temperature can also be determined simultaneously using thermal imaging and laser-induced fluorescence in combination with Rayleigh scattering and the Mach-Zehnder interferometer technique. However, many of these methods are either expensive, bulky, or require complex data analysis, which are significant limitations for their adoption in various applications.

On the other hand, rotational CARS offers a promising approach for the simultaneous determination of temperature, pressure, and composition in gases through a single-shot measurement using an all-solid-state laser system. This technique relies on the detection of signals resulting from the interaction of four laser beams with the molecules in question, at specific wavelengths that are determined by the scalar product of two Raman shifts. Although early implementations of rotational CARS required intricate synchronization of pump and probe pulses and suffered from limited availability of suitable laser systems, recent advancements have made it possible to implement this technique using easily accessible fs/ps laser systems.

We introduce a novel character map called cluster character for the representation theory of quantum groups, specifically those associated with simply-laced types. This character map assigns a polynomial to each irreducible module, reflecting its composition factors' distribution of isomorphism types among the modules' parameterized family, following the structure of Fock-Goncharov's extension of quantum groups through their dual canonical basis. Furthermore, we establish a direct relationship between the coefficients of the cluster character of an irreducible module and the cardinality of its dual canonical basis, demonstrating that this cardinality is encoded in the coefficients of several characters of integrally-closed submodules that share a significant relationship with the module's parameterized family. Lastly, we discover that the dimension character, another feature of quantum groups, can be determined from the cluster characters of its modules. Additionally, we find that the classical limit of the cluster characters of a module's irreducible components smooths out to the dimension character of its classical counterpart. Building upon these findings, we speculate on the connection between the representation theory of quantum groups and the theory of cluster algebras. Finally, we explore how the former's structure, as revealed through the cluster character map, may shape the latter's combinatorial properties. Nonetheless, our research raises more questions than answers, leaving the exploration of these conjectures for future resolution. This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using recent LHC data, specifically focusing on measurements from JADE and CMS experiments. Initially, our findings confirmed the findings of Bartels, Leonidov, and Loewen's work ([1]), but differed in the interpretation. While Bartels et al. found jets to be generated through hard bremsstrahlung processes, we obtained results suggesting jets are primarily hard-scattered partons emitted from the medium, supported by calculations using hard-scattered parton showers. This discrepancy led us to investigate the underlying causes, but no significant differences were found in jet calculations when considering nuclear PDFs, thermal variations of the medium, or changes in the scale. Consequently, the explanation for these results is proposed to stem from the thermal medium affecting hard-scattered partons rather than jets themselves. Furthermore, our research includes an exploration of minimum bias events from CMS, showing no significant changes in the energy spectrum, but reveals distinct medium effects in high-energy jets. Additionally, our analysis highlights the significance of nuclear PDFs in the gluon distribution at low x and Bjorken x values (<0.03), but with much less certainty at higher x values (>0.03). Lastly, our study suggests that CMS and JADE have complementary sensitivity ranges for jet modification, with CMS being more adept at exploring low x values and JADE at examining higher x values (>0.03). In response to a review, the response regarding choice of collider is stated as follows: "Given the current understanding, I would still choose the LHC over a future e+e- or p+p colliders for jet astrophysics, given the higher reachable temperatures and energies that can be achieved with the LHC, specifically at the full 100-100 TeV power of the 7+7 TeV protons." Finally, our research highlights the complex interplay between hard and medium-generated radiation within a medium, leading to the occurrence of overestimation when using jet PDFs, a phenomenon we refer to as the "jet PDF crisis". This "crisis" is shown to be mitigated through the application of hard-scattered parton showers. Moreover, our study proposes the utilization of medium-modified jet functions in conjunction with hard-scattered partons as a more precise approach, offering a new perspective on jet modification within a medium. This perspective is then utilized to analyze medium-modified jet functions using hard-scattered partons at various points, including the origin of the medium, halfway through, and at the exit point

We investigated 19 potential globular clusters within the Milky Way's bulge using infrared images from the VVV survey. Our analysis involved precise position calculations and estimated radii for the potential clusters. Further examination was conducted to distinguish them from likely contaminants, such as RR Lyrae star fields and the bulge's general population, by comparing their density and distribution. Our research utilized various techniques including a Harris profile for density analysis, and we established criteria based on the number of detected variables relative to the estimated radius of each cluster. Our findings identified three promising globular clusters: VVV CLUS-034, with an estimated 1.53 million years based on five RR Lyrae members from photometric data; VVV CLUS-037, with an age estimate of 1.26 billion years from one RR Lyrae member and three Cepheids; and VVV CLUS-062, with an age estimate of 1.26 billion years from one RR Lyrae member and two Cepheids. Additionally, we detected multiple other potential globular clusters within the bulge, including three in the Sagittarius arm and two near the minor axis of the galaxy. These findings contribute to the ongoing debate about the bulge's globular cluster population and may shed light on the early history of the Milky Way. The study finds that quark and gluon wave effects become more pronounced at higher energy scales and above certain momentum thresholds. The study provides insights into the role of quark and gluon interactions in hard scattering processes and the potential for experimental validation through quark and gluon wave effects on boson pair properties. We examine the measurement-based description of light-matter interactions using first-principles tight-binding models. To achieve this, we apply a series of transformations to the TB Hamiltonian, mimicking the interaction between light and matter. Utilizing the measure-indistinguishability theorem, we investigate the impact of measurements on system behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under specific conditions, measurements do not differentiate between system states, thus making some system properties independent of measurements. Consequently, this leads to a distinction between system properties that are robust and those that are not. We refer to the former as persistent and the latter as transient properties. Persistent properties remain unchanged upon variation of system parameters and are characterized by a constant value across measurements, in contrast to transient properties which exhibit a dependent value and can drop below the detection threshold. We associate permanent changes in system spectra with permanent changes in transient properties and temporary changes in system spectra with temporary changes in persistent properties. Notably, permanent changes arise from modifications to the system's permanent dipole moment, whereas temporary changes arise from alterations to the system's temporary dipole moment. Our research provides a foundation for the development of reliable and precise techniques to measure permanent and temporary DC and optical dipole moments of semiconductor microstructures. Additionally, our findings facilitate a deeper understanding of system behavior during measurements and the identification of suitable markers for measuring permanent and temporary DC and optical dipole moments. These markers include the permanent and temporary shifts of system resonances as well as the permanent and temporary changes in system spectra. Our study also highlights the distinction between system properties that are robust and those that are not, enabling more accurate descriptions of light-matter interactions and the measurement process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that transient properties can fall below the detection threshold, which is applicable to the measurement of system properties in the presence of vacuum field fluctuations. To address this issue, we propose using more sensitive detection methods, such as photon detection systems, to measure permanent and temporary properties. Furthermore, we explore the concept of multi-level systems and demonstrate that, in certain conditions, the measurement process can distinguish between system states in a way that is indistinguishable in single-level systems. This leads to a more comprehensive understanding of the measurement process in complex systems. Our research also reveals that the measurement process can result in a persistent change in system behavior, which is a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics. The rising popularity of Learning from Log Data techniques stems from their ability to create predictive models by analyzing past process behavior, thus enabling the estimation and forecasting of future process activity. Despite widespread adoption, research into underlying questions remains limited. This paper addresses these inquiries by comparing common deep-learning approaches for extrapolating past data and constructing predictive models of future process behavior. We evaluate seven prominent models – RNN, LSTM, GRU, Transformer, Attention-based VA, Semi-SVNN, and Zero-shot SVNN – in terms of their ability to extend past data and predict future process behavior. Our results reveal that simple RNN and LSTM models often perform better than complex, optimized versions for both extrapolation and prediction tasks. Moreover, we discover that models capable of analyzing only past data perform as well as those that can analyze both past and future information for certain metrics. Additionally, our findings indicate that certain models can produce unsatisfactory results due to their tendency to overfit, thus highlighting the need for additional evaluation metrics that assess a model's ability to balance accuracy and reliability. We also introduce two new open datasets – DPCOS – to facilitate further research into process modeling, extrapolation, and forecasting. We anticipate that our study will facilitate a deeper understanding of the capabilities and limitations of modern deep-learning models for process forecasting and guide future research in this area. In addition, we have made all model implementations and evaluation results openly available to facilitate further exploration of these complex topics. Microblogging platforms like Twitter offer valuable insights into disaster relief efforts and public opinion, which can be obtained through social mirror APIs but are no longer available due to licensing costs and data privacy concerns. Alternatively, firehose access to Twitter data via streaming APIs can be acquired but requires expensive licensing. Conversely, Twitter Advanced Search allows for free access to relevant data posted before the cutting-off point, which can be achieved using the "until" parameter. This paper presents an approach to acquiring and analyzing Twitter data utilizing Twitter Advanced Search. The analysis focuses on the 2020 Izmir earthquake in Turkey and encompasses an examination of posted data along with relief efforts and public opinion analysis. The results demonstrate that this method is an effective and economical way to acquire Twitter data. Furthermore, the data and insights obtained can contribute to the development of more accurate disaster relief scenarios. The data and code utilized in this research are made freely available for other researchers to utilize. The latter consisted of around 327 individual videos posted by users, out of which around 17% were uploaded by around 50 different users. A massive eruption occurred on April 12, 1985, on the surface of the active G9.5Ve star AD Leo, emitting a huge amount of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum from radio to gamma rays and creating a massive particle flux that interacted strongly with the solar system. This event, which affected the upper atmosphere of Mars and caused a noticeable increase in the planet's debris ring, also generated an enormous UV flux that could have impacted low-orbit spacecraft. Despite extensive research on this event, previous studies have focused mainly on high-energy observations and atmospheric interactions, while the near-UV component, which could have significantly affected low-orbit spacecraft, has gone largely unexamined. To address this gap, a simulation model has been developed to recreate the near-UV spectrum of the eruption based on existing white-light observations and flux measurements in other spectral ranges. This simulation demonstrates that the eruption's ultra-violet continuum showed a significant excess beyond what would be expected from the star's normal spectral energy distribution, exhibiting a shallow power law and approximately following the same shape as the optical component while exceeding it in intensity. This excess in UV flux has been confirmed by existing measurements from the NIMBUS-7 satellite, which detected a significant increase in UV radiation at 283 nanometers during the eruption. This simulation model can simulate complex white-light structures observed during the eruption and has implications for enhancing detection capabilities of similar events that may cause charges in spacecraft memory, such as the one documented in this paper for the spacecraft Rosetta, to improve the likelihood of identifying such events in the future. Additionally, this model can also be adapted to derive flare intensities at spacecraft distances, a key factor in assessing the threat to spacecraft by flares. This approach to the problem, which involves the derivation of integral flare densities from structural and flux measurements, is not only applicable to UV continuum but also extends with necessary modifications to other spectral ranges including optical, X-ray, and radio. This approach to the problem, which involves the incorporation of observational constraints into theoretical models, also has a broader significance in scientific research as it highlights the importance of a systematic approach to the solution of complex scientific problems that may involve various datasets measured with different methods over long periods and at different spatial extensions, and the need for a careful examination of the results obtained with the new method against all available data, followed by a thorough validation of the method on known events before applying it to detection of transients in data that were previously missed. This has a significant significance in an era of giant telescopes

We're investigating medium access control (MAC) techniques in frequency-modulation continuous-wave (FMCW) radar networks to prevent interference between radars. Typically, FMCW radars utilize a unique code to identify their returned signals, enabling them to detect and avoid collisions. However, generating and managing these unique codes can be challenging, particularly in systems with many radars. To address this issue, we're analyzing the performance of existing wireless communication network protocols, such as ALOHA and CSMA, to find solutions for designing radar systems with high reliability and minimal delays. To this end, we've developed a protocol based on ALOHA, called slotted ALOHA, and one based on CSMA, called CSMA, and evaluated their efficiency under different code design approaches. Our findings provide valuable insights for the safe and efficient operation of FMCW radar networks in the presence of overlapping transmission periods. Moreover, the code design strategies we've explored, namely time-hopping and direct sequencing, prove useful in managing the radars' behavior. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that properly designed wireless communication networks can be adapted for use in radar systems with FMCW technology. Additionally, our code design strategies are applicable across a broad spectrum of radar frequencies. To facilitate further exploration, we've developed a code available on GitHub under an permissive license. However, it's essential to note that this work is theoretical and experimental validation is necessary. Furthermore, while our solution is adaptable to various frequency ranges, each specific application may require its own customized code modification. As a result, we've provided the underlying principles of our code, giving other researchers a head start in its further development. In the future, our findings can be expanded to other types of radar systems as well as diverse wireless communication networks. On the other hand, some experts might argue that the scope of this research is too narrow, but we disagree with this assessment. On the issue of code modification, it's true that our approach is system-specific, but this decision was deliberate, given the fundamental differences between radar systems and standard communication networks. While it's possible to develop more general code modification strategies, they would likely result in suboptimal performance. Instead, we recommend that each unique application or system develop its own tailored solution.
