To address this issue, this paper introduces the Pied Piper system, an innovative solution that uses a carefully crafted set of general questions to locate the most reliable and precise information about a specific song across the web. This system leverages the latest advancements in natural language processing and machine learning to evaluate the credibility of the information found, using an example dataset of 2000 songs to develop a general meta-query to determine the most accurate classification for a given song. Furthermore, Pied Piper's unique approach enables it to efficiently handle real-world challenges like songs with multiple artists, as well as adapt to changing data conditions and biases. LiDAR technology equips vehicles with precise sensors to scan and map their surroundings in 3D. Although the data they collect appears complex and intricate, the majority of current approaches to analyzing this data rely on the use of feature extractors which, despite effectiveness, can be costly in large-scale settings. Alternatively, learning-based methods have been explored for tasks such as detection, classification, and mapping, with numerous successful applications; however, the field lacks a comprehensive overview of LiDAR-specific techniques. The standard technique for evaluating integrals on the sphere - by transforming to polar coordinates and then integrating - faces a complication when trying to calculate an average value. Due to the intricate nature of the delta function in polar coordinates, this method is not feasible. Alternatively, we propose a one-step method for calculating averages and moments of functions on the sphere by utilizing a specific delta function in equatorial coordinates. This approach allows us to derive the desired properties and a new formula for the Dirichlet distribution on the sphere. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to the evaluation of integrals and expected values of functions of spherical polynomials. Furthermore, we investigate the statistical properties of spherical polynomials and their ability to capture the variability of geometric data on the sphere. We also examine the relationship between our method and traditional approaches, as well as the advantages of our one-step strategy. The results show that the proposed method is more efficient and easier to implement than the standard techniques. The paper concludes with an exploration of possible extensions and applications of the one-step method. The results and the approach can be generalized to higher-dimensional spaces, such as the hypersphere, and the paper also discusses the potential for answering questions and the tools for the evaluation of the proposed method in these higher-dimensional spaces. The discovery of neutrino events by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory has generated significant interest in identifying the sources of ultra-high-energy cosmic particles. By analyzing 12 years of data, this research seeks to uncover connections between neutrino arrival directions and the distribution of these cosmic particles across the sky. Our study reveals a perceived link between neutrino ensembles and high-energy cosmic rays within 2 degrees of radius, which holds a statistical significance of 4.8 sigma in favor of the hypothesis. This association, however, disappears when considering larger radii of 10 degrees. Notably, the observed correlation between neutrinos and cosmic rays within 2 degrees strengthens the significance of previously reported instances of spatial connections between neutrinos and high-energy cosmic particles from all angles. This finding further supports the notion that many high-energy cosmic sources are located in dense regions rich with cosmic rays, and that such environments are conducive to accelerating particles to ultra-high energies. Moreover, this association raises the intriguing possibility that about 20% of detected high-energy cosmic particles might originate from these spatial connections with neutrinos, which would significantly enhance the overall neutrino flux as detected by IceCube. Nonetheless, this interpretation holds little significance if the observed correlation is primarily attributed to a cosmic ray contamination within neutrino selection. Moreover, our study for the first time uses a comprehensive approach to identify spatial associations between neutrinos and cosmic particles, which has implications for the interpretation of future joint analyses of these cosmic phenomena. Furthermore, this research has implications for the development of markers that could aid in identifying true neutrino sources within such analyses. Additionally, our results have implications for the study of cosmic ray nuclei and photons in other energy ranges, which could be sensitive to the same high-energy cosmic sources. The flow of a liquid through a narrow channel is influenced by two opposing forces: the pressure difference driving the liquid and the resistance it encounters. In a liquid foam, this resistance is primarily caused by two types of obstacles: the curved surfaces of bubbles and the irregularities along the channel's walls. While the effects of curved surfaces on fluid flow have been extensively studied, the impact of surface roughness remains less understood, especially in fluid flows with high surface tensions. In our research, we focused on the flow of a liquid through a narrow channel with a high liquid surface tension, where the effects of curved surfaces are minimized. By mapping the flow resistance in a liquid foam at various tensions and densities, we were able to show that the resistance it poses is mainly determined by the roughness of the surface and the curvature of the bubbles, and that it is only significantly affected by the presence of very low-curvature bubbles in the channel. The results of our research have implications for our understanding of flow resistance in various materials and can be applied to the design of devices that manage the flow of liquids in porous media, such as oil recovery and the management of water in soil. The steady-state fingering pattern that develops around a slowly moving bubble in a rectangular box filled with a different liquid, when the bubble is tilted, has been the subject of various studies. Research is extended to the case where the bubble is curved and moves slowly in a rectangular box filled with a different liquid, both with and without being tilted. The spread of the faster liquid forms a curved front around the bubble, which is stable and branched when the bubble is tilted and curved, respectively. The branched structure shares similarities with the Hansen-Yorke structure found in Rayleigh-Benard convection, and both are influenced by a dimensionless box aspect ratio. The boundary between these two states in the Rayleigh-Benard and Hele-Shaw systems both follow an "egg-chicken" problem, where the behavior depends on the relationship between two factors that determine them, and both become less stable as the box aspect ratio increases from its most compact to its most expansive extreme. The curvatures of the branched structure and the bubble are directly related, and both are influenced by the same "egg-chicken" problem, resulting in the coexistence of two "islands" of either stable or branched states when the bubble's curvature is negative or positive, respectively. The boundary between these "islands" breaks into two "seas" when the bubble's curvature is zero, and both "islands" shrink and eventually disappear when the box is either too compact or too expansive. The behavior of the Hele-Shaw system can be understood through a simple model that represents the spread of the faster liquid as the movement of a surface in the direction of the faster liquid, and both this model and research on the case where the bubble is tilted provide insight into the "egg-chicken" problem. The concept of Hamiltonian dynamics remains a cornerstone in the development of canonical and symplectic numerical integration methods. Despite its numerous benefits, the major limitation of these methods lies in their inability to handle large time steps due to the preservation of the symplectic form. This constraint arises from the preservation of the phase space volume, which essentially limits the size of the time steps. This research introduces an innovative approach that bypasses this volume preservation alteration. We leverage the unconstrained Hamiltonian Hamiltonian integration method previously proposed by Cela and Leimkuhler, and modify it to directly utilize the Hamiltonian-based time step determination procedure. By doing so, we successfully eliminate the need for an additional Hamiltonian preservation step. This new method is thoroughly analyzed and validated through a range of challenging tests for both conservative and dissipative systems. The results show a significant improvement in the allowed time step when compared to the standard symplectic method, without compromising precision. Additionally, we explore the implications of this method for multi-sphere problems and demonstrate its applicability. This new approach offers a crucial breakthrough in the development of more efficient and precise numerical integration methods for Hamiltonian systems over extended time periods. This breakthrough is also highlighted by a related discovery made during the course of this research, which is the inspection of the Hamiltonian-based time step determination procedure's behavior in conjunction with the unconstrained expansion method. This insight, although established through the study of a simple one-dimensional Hamiltonian system, may have more comprehensive implications in the context of multi-dimensional Hamiltonian dynamics. This is because the time step determination procedure is directly linked to the initial conditions of each degree of freedom. This relationship could potentially allow for the optimization of time steps in multi-dimensional problems, a feature that may be explored in future research. This new method, combined with the ability to utilize an expanded Hamiltonian pathway, offers a crucial opportunity to further optimize time steps in a variety of applications. This is especially true in scenarios where the Hamiltonian varies little across the time step, as demonstrated by the included benchmark tests. In neural generation models, particularly those with attention mechanisms, 
the practice of "look-ahead" or "future-aware" processing has been observed.
This phenomenon is illustrated through a case study involving neural 
machine translation, where an analysis of the data reveals that the 
distribution of attention weights tends to concentrate on segments of the 
source sentence associated with the proposed creation in the target sentence.
This focus on future-aware processing is shown to be a generally applicable 
pattern across multiple language pairs and is corroborated by explicit 
queries regarding the intended reference. A qualitative analysis of the 
results suggests that the implied understanding of the source sentence is 
often more comprehensive than what is understood locally, within individual 
phrasal units. As a consequence, the proposed framework of the paper 
emphasizes the importance of modeling a longer-range, forward-oriented 
perspective in the learning process, leading to the introduction of a 
novel neural network architecture that incorporates a look-ahead focus 
mechanism. This new architecture, where a second attention mechanism is 
introduced to model the intended creation, is compared to the standard 
neural machine translation baseline, revealing improved performance on both 
metric-based evaluation and human assessment. The improved capabilities 
of the model are further demonstrated through the results of a second 
task, where it is applied to a creation task within a summarization context.

The experience of developing a grid computing testbed at the University of Hawaii was shared with European Natioanl Research and Education Network (NREN) stakeholders to guide the translation of the lessons learned into practical advice for similar large-scale infrastructure projects. A key takeaway from this exercise was the value of a translational approach in research, which was not initially considered a primary focus of the project. However, the challenges encountered while developing the Pacific Grid motivated a refinement of the research methodology to involve the simultaneous development of the grid infrastructure and applications that could be run on it. This revised approach to research is an example of a translational research methodology, which offers several advantages over more traditional methods. The experience with the Pacific Grid also highlights the importance of a robust infrastructure development framework, which supports the creation of complex, distributed systems. Finally, the opportunity to share the approach to developing the Pacific Grid with international stakeholders has led to a refinement of the methodology and a more general framework for developing large-scale, distributed infrastructure. This revised framework addresses the challenges associated with such projects and could be adapted to address the issues related to cloud computing. The development of the Pacific Grid also demonstrated the value of a grid computing approach over more traditional methods for supporting large-scale, distributed research collaborations. This study introduces a groundbreaking, multi-faceted approach to analyzing student curiosity during small group learning sessions. Combining automatic detection of curiosity expressions and individual interest assessments with observational data of learning behaviors and environmental factors, this method reveals the complex dynamics of curiosity in this setting. To demonstrate its effectiveness, this study uses the developed framework to investigate how individual curiosity and interest levels influence each other, as well as the impact of external factors, such as instructor guidance, on curiosity in a real-world scenario. Findings from a case study on elementary school students' science learning reveal surprising insights into the temporal curiosity dynamics and the varying effects of internal and external factors, confirming the significance of considering both in the comprehensive study of curiosity in small group learning. This research validates the value of this method in producing valuable insights and shows that complex temporal data analysis can be achieved with appropriate preprocessing of curiosity expression data. This study provides a valuable contribution to the advancement of learning science research and can be applied to the evaluation of learning systems that aim to stimulate curiosity in educational settings. Gaussian processes serve as a fundamental tool for assessing uncertainty in various applications.  However, their inherent limitation is the inability to efficiently compute predictions for complex functions within large datasets.  A promising strategy to overcome this challenge involves using Mat\'ern Gaussian processes, which can produce smoother function predictions.  This paper extends the capabilities of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to analyze data on complex relationships by incorporating kernel functions based on graph signals.  A theoretical framework is provided to ensure these kernel functions comply with established criteria, facilitating Mat\'ern Gaussian process applications.  Our approach is a novel contribution to the field, as previous studies have only explored RBF kernel functions within Gaussian processes but not Mat\'ern Gaussian processes.  Through both analytical and numerical experiments, our results demonstrate the efficacy and performance of Mat\'ern Gaussian processes compared to RBF Gaussian processes.  Furthermore, our findings show that by incorporating kernel derivatives, Mat\'ern Gaussian processes can yield better predictive models, especially in scenarios with noise-free data.  In contrast, RBF Gaussian processes may not always outperform Mat\'ern Gaussian processes, underscoring the significance of choosing an appropriate Gaussian process model for a given problem.  Our research provides a groundbreaking answer to the question of whether RBF Gaussian processes can be optimal solutions, as we demonstrate that this optimality depends on the specific graph at hand.  Our study paves the way for a broader exploration of kernel research in the context of Gaussian processes.  In conclusion, this paper makes a substantial contribution to the field by establishing a theoretical framework and novel results that will inspire further research and provide valuable insights for experts working with Gaussian processes and kernel functions.  Our results have important implications and can be of significant use to those working with Gaussian processes, graph signals, and kernel functions. The optimal placement of sensors within a city's road system network is a critical issue, particularly in areas where ridesharing vehicles frequently operate. In this study, a comprehensive model is established that can determine the minimum number of sensing devices required to accurately identify all roads within the city, using a database of commonly visited locations associated with ridesharing vehicles. Our analysis aims to identify the subset of most frequently traversed roads that covers the majority of the city, using techniques such as matroid theory and greedy algorithms. Our results, based on real-world data from New York City and Chicago, show that only a small percentage of roads in these cities need to be equipped with sensing devices, covering more than 90% of the city's area with an accuracy of less than 5% error. This research could be applied to various urban monitoring applications, such as optimizing road maintenance and managing urban weather conditions. In addition, we introduce an interactive visualization tool, known as UrbanCoverage, that can be used to explore the results and solutions to this problem in an intuitive manner. This tool enables users to easily add or remove roads from the solution and observe the associated coverage changes. Furthermore, our research and the associated dashboard can be adapted to accommodate other urban road systems networks. In addition to detecting city roads, this problem has a broader connection to the minimum hit set problem, a well-known computational mathematics problem. In this study, we also introduce an efficient and effective algorithm, known as the Reduced Dimensional Thickness First (RDTF) algorithm, that can resolve this issue more efficiently than the existing state-of-the-art methods. In particular, our experiments indicate that the RDTF algorithm can determine an optimal solution in real-world scenarios, such as the New York City and Chicago urban road systems, approximately 5 to 7 times faster than the current industry standard. This new algorithm, along with the associated code and the UrbanCoverage dashboard, can be accessed via the publicly available GitHub repository https://github.com/AmirHoushiar/UrbanCoverage, and a demonstration of the dashboard can be found at https://video.itt.ac/video/617e2b0a-7f3f-4c3f-8c5c-1f1f0f1f1f1f. This study determines the global persistence probability for a one-dimensional stochastic walk as it relates to its local duration in a finite time frame. To achieve this, we first establish an exact, high-resolution probability distribution for the local persistence of various types of one-dimensional stochastic walks, including simple random walks, biased walks, walk-with-turns, and biased walk-with-turns. Building upon these findings, we derive the global persistence probability as the exponential decay of the local persistence probability with a dependent mean lifetime. Notably, the resulting global persistence probability matches existing theories for large values of the walk rate or number of possible turn directions. Additionally, we demonstrate the accuracy of our approach by comparing our results to existing literature. Furthermore, our high-resolution distribution of local persistence provides insight into the underlying reasons for the exponential decay of global persistence probability. Lastly, we conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for understanding the global persistence probability in complex systems.

Computer-based automatic nucleus detection can aid in reducing costs and improving efficiency in cancer diagnosis by streamlining the processing of histopathological images. However, the presence of varied staining patterns, overlapping cells, and non-uniform lighting in these images poses significant challenges for nucleus detection. To address these issues, we developed a dual-stage Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) called W-Net, which is composed of two stages: a primary stage that uses a standard CNN to identify potential nucleus regions, followed by a refinement stage that utilizes a Thin-Plate Spline (TPS) regression-based DenseNet to verify and validate the identified regions. W-Net's capacity to accurately identify nucleus regions in various cancer types, including liver, colon, and breast cancers, has been validated through extensive experiments. However, as with all deep learning-based solutions, the reliance on substantial training datasets remains a concern. To address this issue, our group is exploring the application of limited-label learning techniques for the W-Net model. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome, which forms a bridge (called a "pore") in infected cell membranes, leading to the release of cytokines. Research into possible treatments for COVID-19 has identified several that can prevent the formation of the NLRP3 inflammasome or the release of cytokines. To analyze and predict the effectiveness of such treatments, we developed a mathematical model that tracks the formation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, pyroptotic cell death, and the associated release of cytokines. Our model indicates that treatments preventing the formation of the NLRP3 inflammasome or the release of cytokines can significantly decrease cytokine levels, while treatments that delay the pore's formation or cell death may be less effective in reducing cytokine levels immediately, but could still be beneficial in the long run by reducing the total amount of cytokines released from a single cell over time. Our research also demonstrates that the rate of cell death through pyroptosis can influence the balance of cytokine release and that some treatments that increase this rate may not necessarily be beneficial in the short term. Our model is a single-cell model and does not account for the communication between cells, which can still be an area of further mathematical modeling. Our research does, however, provide a foundation for further exploration into how treatments for pyroptosis-induced inflammation could be optimized. In our research, we take a critical look at the widespread use of modular systems in multi-task reinforcement learning. While these architectures are frequently employed due to their capacity to balance trade-offs between multiple tasks in a complex environment, the real benefit might stem from their ability to prevent performance deterioration when a single task presents a significant obstacle. To investigate this hypothesis, we introduce the concept of a difficult task as one whose optimal policy is vastly inferior to the optimal policies for the other tasks, resulting in a solution that is far from ideal for the entire system. We then present a series of challenging tasks designed to assess the effectiveness of various reinforcement learning architectures when confronted with a difficult task. Our findings consistently show that modular systems consistently perform better than non-modular alternatives, confirming our initial hypothesis. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the advantage of modular systems can be understood through the lens of catastrophe escape, where a difficult task raises significant barriers to learning from trial and error, and that this insight yields valuable insights into the design of reinforcement learning components. To facilitate further exploration of the intricacies of multi-task reinforcement learning, we also introduce the concept of a hard transition as a raised barrier to optimal policy execution and provide an accompanying dataset of difficult transitions available for download. Overall, our research underlines the value of incorporating modular systems into complex reinforcement learning environments to mitigate the risk of suboptimal performance. The method we propose, Consecutive Spatially Equitable Sampling (CSES), is an advancement of the well-known Equitable Sharing (EQS) strategy. Our approach builds upon previous research by allowing users to tap into location-based content as they navigate through it, leveraging their current position in the dataset. Moreover, through experimental evaluations using real-world datasets, we demonstrate that CSES not only guarantees equitable sharing but also outperforms existing methods in terms of retrieval precision and user satisfaction. The equitable sharing constraint of one item per user per time step can be overcome by allowing users to select consecutive items. This modification enhances the efficacy of the EQS algorithm, especially in scenarios where items are closely spaced and offer similar values to users. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in two applications: searching for and grasping an object and assessing damage on an complex robotic assembly. We also explore ways to further improve our method by incorporating additional training and adapting it for use in sealed environments. Our technique has the potential to contribute to the development of more user-friendly and robust robotic systems in various industries. Next-generation wireless networks demand extremely high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face significant absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop LiDAR/RF hybrid communications to extend the communication range, albeit these systems involve time-consuming beam training processes that can limit the performance of scheduling algorithms. To address this challenge, we developed a novel reinforcement learning-based approach known as the Hybrid Beam Training (HBT) policy, which optimizes the beam training process in each individual hop by prioritizing maximum forward progress. With the HBT policy, the average number of training requests needed is shown to be directly proportional to the (1+1)p-log of the number of possible training options, where p represents the penetration depth of the environment. Moreover, we derived the general form of the HBT policy under different reward settings and verified its effectiveness through numerical simulations and real-world experiments using a custom-built THz communication setup. The results show that the HBT policy can achieve up to 5.5 Gbps data transfer rates over distances of up to 10 meters in an office environment. The surroundings of nearby pulsars can offer insights into the local interstellar medium. Researching the line of sight to these pulsars is essential as it can provide details about the medium and possible structures in the solar neighborhood. This study focuses on the pulsar B1133+16, located 797 pc from Earth, to explore its surroundings and the scattering of its radio waves. By analyzing scintillation patterns, the team discovered two distinct components at 810 MHz, including a wide angular spread of approximately 13 minutes of arc, and several smaller features. Modeling these components as separate screens, the team found their separations to be about 11.4 arcmin, and their angular sizes to be 12.3 and 1.08 minutes of arc, respectively. This research also revealed significant structure in the line of sight to B1133+16, and by assuming a screen at a distance of 800 pc, the team was able to use it as a lens to calculate the mass of a possible dark star or black hole, or a white dwarf with a large cooling spot, or even an unseen pulsar with a massive dim magnetosphere, however more frequent and detailed monitoring is needed to confirm these findings and increase precision. This research also brought forward a method to determine the distance to these screens by analyzing the frequency-dependent wide scintillation structure, and a potential hidden structure at a closer distance to B1133+16, which could be validated by very long baseline interferometry. This discovery provides a basis for further study of the pulsar population to understand the local interstellar medium, and the team recommends the use of wide-field scintillation studies as an effective and cost-effective approach for this kind of research. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that by utilizing a radio telescope at Arecibo and a network of radio telescopes across the globe, it is possible to accomplish wide-field scintillation studies of distant pulsars. This approach, however, is limited by the large field of view that can be covered by these telescopes, and the time it takes to move the telescope to a new direction, and therefore, a telescope with a wide field of view, such as the Square Kilometre Array, will be more suitable and more effective in this kind of research. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks (CNNs). WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of global context within each layer hinders the model's ability to produce quasi-periodic signals like speech and music. We address this issue by introducing a pitch-sensitive dilated CNN, where the dilation sizes follow a quasi-periodic pattern, thereby preserving global context. This innovative architecture is then integrated into a WaveNet-like framework called QPNet, with two structures being explored and their performance evaluated using objective quality assessment metrics. The results indicate that both QPNet variants outperform the baseline WN and a modified dilated convolution network, with one of these QPNet variants exhibiting performance on par with a highly complex 31-layer WN model. The models' performance is analyzed through runtime and parameter count considerations. Furthermore, a pre-trained QPNet model's pitch-synthesis capabilities are examined by conducting a set of pitch manipulation tests. Developing and fine-tuning machine learning models for Arabic language tasks encounter significant challenges due to the lack of standardized morphological annotations and spelling corrections. This issue stems from the complex nature of Arabic script and morphology, compounded by the limited availability of well-annotated corpora. To address this problem, we present MADARi, an online platform designed to facilitate collaborative annotation and spelling correction of Arabic texts through a set of carefully crafted web tools. By providing a user-friendly interface and clear guidance for annotators, MADARi aims to enable the creation of high-quality annotated corpora in an efficient and cost-effective manner. This approach allows researchers to leverage the expertise of which-ever annotators are available, regardless of their geographical location. By utilizing a flexible schema that supports multiple annotator roles and a peer-review process, MADARi ensures the accuracy and reliability of the produced annotations. Furthermore, our implementation of a web-based data storage system and annotator interface built using popular open-source technologies enables seamless integration with popular deep learning frameworks, such as Hugging Face Transformers. To illustrate the effectiveness of MADARi, we present the results of fine-tuning the BERT-Arabic model on a spellchecking task using a dataset annotated through our web platform. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of MADARi to create high-quality annotated datasets, enabling researchers to develop and fine-tune machine learning models for various Arabic language tasks. By leveraging this web platform, we believe that it is now feasible to tackle complex NLP tasks in Arabic. We invite other researchers to explore the capabilities of MADARi and contribute to the expansion of which-ever annotated datasets they utilize in their research. We also provide a sample annotation guide and spellchecking dataset created through MADARi, available at which-ever URLs. We are open to receiving feedback and suggestions from which-ever researchers wish to collaborate with us. This project was funded by which-ever institution. Planetary photochemistry plays a key role in identifying biomarkers and other atmospheric features in exoplanet spectra, making it essential to study this process across various planetary conditions. This study explores how gas-rich exoplanets with temperatures between -10°C and 50°C interact with their host stars' radiant energy, specifically focusing on hazy atmospheres that impede radiation from reaching depths beyond 1 bar and transfer depths of 10-100 bar. We introduce an adjustable finite element method for solving the second-order diffusion equation. This method can be used for problems with rapidly changing coefficients, provided the variations are gradual, typically found in time-harmonic wave propagation and scattering problems. Our technique involves two main components: a mesh-based approach and a series of increasingly refined sub-domains. Initially, problems with rough diffusion coefficients are approximated through a mesh-based method such as the Galerkin finite element method. However, this can lead to initial solution inaccuracy, especially when the coefficients change suddenly. To address this, we employ an iterative strategy, where the solution is progressively refined within each sub-domain until it satisfies given a priori estimates. This results in a more accurate solution, although the process can be computationally expensive due to the repeated assembly of finite element matrices. Ultimately, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this adjustable finite element method, first theoretically, and then through a series of numerical experiments, including examples of time-harmonic Maxwell's equations. The implementation of this method is also examined, and potential further developments such as the use of non-matching interfaces between sub-domains are also discussed. The adjustable finite element method can lead to significantly improved solution accuracy, especially in problems with large jumps in diffusion coefficients, although further work is needed to fully utilize its potential. Recently discovered water contents in the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites provide evidence for extensive water accumulation within inner solar system planetesimals during the formation of the solar system. Our research offers a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon, suggesting that the water was derived from the solar nebula, partially in a molecular form, combined with the neutralizing effects of volatile-rich silicate minerals, particularly orthopyroxene, brucite, and phyllosilicates, which reduced the pH level, allowing the formation of hydrated silicate minerals such as pyroxene and phyllosilicates through gas-solid reactions, followed by the hydrothermal alteration of igneous rocks, resulting in the formation of hydrous minerals such as amphibole, mica, and talc. This process is supported by various evidence, including isotopic analysis, thermometry through the composition of apatite, and petrographic analysis, which demonstrate a combination of magmatic and hydrothermal processes, in addition to volatile excesses reflected in the orthopyroxene composition, particularly the content of oxygen isotopes, which show a D$_{\rm punit}$ value of -47.5. Furthermore, our research suggests that the water contents in the Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites are consistent with the average water content of inner solar system meteorites, estimated at approximately 0.25 water mass fraction, in mass units of Earth's water, which may have originated from the solar nebula, amounting to about 1.5 Earth water masses, with the majority lost due to planet formation, leaving behind a small, terrestrial planet with low water content, such as Earth. This research provides a comprehensive explanation for the extensive water accumulation within inner solar system planetesimals, offering alternative hypotheses to dismiss the validity of recent studies, including those published in the journal Icarus in 2020, Volume 347, Article ID 114299, and in the planetary science journal Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors in 2021, Volume 311, Article ID 106694.

This task is significant because it demands the ability to link auditory inputs to both visual and linguistic information. We develop two datasets to support this task: a basic set featuring general descriptions of images and a more complex set featuring detailed instructions on enhancing photos. Our experiments reveal that significant advancements are possible by combining the guidelines with high-quality image descriptions and utilizing pre-trained models incorporating contrastive learning. A particular model we examined, a 14-layer vision transformer, achieves remarkable performance on both datasets. Notably, it executes the instructions in the complex dataset with an accuracy of 73.1%, outperforming human performance. Moreover, our findings indicate that the instructions given to the model can be understood by human observers, even when the model's descriptions differ from the instructions. This understanding raises questions about the model's interpretation of the instructions and its description of the images. This conclusion is based on the observation that the model's performance on the complex dataset improves when the instructions are clear and the images are well-described. This improvement suggests the model's capability to execute complex instructions successfully. We conduct an human evaluation of the model's audio descriptions of videos, using both automatic and human-generated descriptions as comparators. This expansion serves as a standard for the validity of approximate methods, such as the dipolar approximation, and can be employed to identify relevant parameters, including the characteristic length of the multipolar series, which dictates accuracy and computational efficiency. Our approach also facilitates the expansion of complex optical properties, such as nonlocal and nonlinear responses, and can be adapted for interacting systems by developing a framework for the multipolar interaction, this work specifically focuses on the analysis of individual nanoscale objects. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of this approach to an assortment of objects, including dimers, rods, and spheres, and show that even beyond the long wavelength regime, the dipolar approximation yields manageable cross-section values, albeit with inherent overestimation. In contrast, the accuracy of the optical torque calculation is significantly more sensitive to the specific multipolar series and is heavily dependent on the shape of the object in question. Ultimately, this work provides a framework for evaluating the validity and potential applications of approximate methods used in the calculation of optical properties of nanoscale objects. Additionally, we have discovered that the widely used static dipolar approximation for scattering calculations yields reasonable results for objects with a large characteristic size (several hundred nanometers) across all wavelengths, while for smaller objects (around 100 nanometers) and specific resonant frequencies, a dynamic dipolar calculation is advised. On the other hand, the dynamic dipolar approximation for optical torque calculations proves to be accurate only for objects with a characteristic size of at least 100 nanometers. Conversely, for smaller objects, particularly those with a size of around 20 nanometers, the static dipolar approximation actually yields better results. Furthermore, our work establishes an intriguing relationship between the quantum immanent Schur algebra and the classical U(q)-algebra, as well as revealing the underlying connection between the quantum immanent Schur basis and the classical Fock-Lukashevich basis of U(q)-algebra, which is both visually and conceptually striking. Ultimately, our research on these new categories of quantum immanents is expected to contribute positively to the broader theory of quantum immanents. This research investigates how certain categorical invariants in symplectic geometry, specifically relative quantum homology, behave under a specific type of symplectic transformation known as a rational transformation. We have identified and established properties for the relative quantum homology in this context, including the preservation of its structural components and its ring structure. Additionally, this research explores the relationship between relative quantum homology and another invariant, both in its absolute and relative forms, demonstrating their connection in a categorical sense. A key aspect of this investigation is the demonstration that relative quantum homology can be an expansive and dynamic invariant, as exemplified through the case study of the toric variety, which reveals a vastly more complex and intricate structure than its combinatorial description might suggest. A significant contribution of this research is the provision of precise and detailed answers to previously open questions regarding the behavior of quantum homology, particularly in relation to its expansion and contraction properties. Furthermore, this research introduces a new concept, your 'local degree', a term that was initially coined in the course of this investigation. This term will likely be of use in any exploration of the behavior of (relative) quantum homology in the context of local changes, which will very likely be a subject of interest in the study of quantum homology in the future. Lastly, this research establishes a new connection between the expanded form of quantum homology, known as the full Fourier transform of the relative quantum homology, and another invariant known as the topological field theory, which is itself a Fourier transform of a type of symplectic invariant. This new understanding will very likely be a valuable resource for anyone studying the properties of quantum homology and its behavior in response to different symplectic transformations.
